lessons.title: Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation
lessons.summary: LOOCV is k-fold cross-validation taken to the extreme (k = n): each observation is left out once for validation while the model trains on the other n − 1. Covers the definition and terminology, the step-by-step cycle, the loss formula, worked classification (5 students) and regression (MAE) examples, why it uses data efficiently, advantages and limitations, bias–variance intuition, computational cost versus k-fold, a comparison table, a when-to-use decision guide, leakage-safe practice, and a scikit-learn LeaveOneOut implementation.

content.text: One out, every time

Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) takes cross-validation to its extreme: instead of a handful of folds, it makes one fold per observation. The model trains on every record except one, predicts that single left-out case, and repeats until every observation has had its turn — squeezing the maximum training data out of a small dataset.

content.caption: Figure 1. The core idea: train on all observations except one, test on the omitted observation, and repeat n times — then average all the test losses.

content.text: LOOCV trains the model n times, leaving out a different single observation each time, and averages the n validation results.
content.title: One-sentence definition

content.text: These notes stay focused on LOOCV. Other validation methods appear only for direct comparison and concept clarification.
content.title: Scope

content.text: Definition and central idea

A special form of cross-validation where a dataset of n observations is divided into n folds. In each fold, exactly one observation is used for validation while the remaining n − 1 observations train the model.
Key characteristics

items: Number of folds: k = n (the total number of observations).
Training set per fold: n − 1 observations.
Validation set per fold: 1 observation.
Number of model fits: n separate fits.
Final result: the average loss, accuracy, or error across all n folds.

content.text: Terminology

rows: One data record, row, sample, or instance.
One iteration in which a particular observation is left out.
The single observation used for validation in that fold.
All remaining n − 1 observations used to fit the model.
The error for the left-out case (e.g. squared error or 0/1 loss).
The mean of the n individual validation losses or scores.

content.text: How LOOCV works

items: Prepare the dataset — assume it has n observations.
Select one observation — temporarily remove observation i.
Train the model — fit on the other n − 1 observations.
Test the model — predict the target for the single left-out observation.
Record performance — store its error or whether the prediction was correct.
Repeat — choose a different observation until every one has been tested once.
Average the results — the mean of all n losses is the LOOCV estimate.

content.caption: Figure 2. LOOCV folds for a dataset with 6 observations — each row leaves one observation out for testing: six observations → six model fits → six predictions → one averaged score.
Figure 3. The train–predict–record cycle repeats until every observation has been left out once, then the losses are averaged.

content.text: Mathematical form

content.explanation: f⁽⁻ⁱ⁾ is the model trained without observation i, and L measures the error on that left-out observation. For classification, L is often 0/1 loss; for regression, absolute or squared error.

content.text: Worked example: classification
A small dataset has five students; the task is to predict pass (1) or fail (0). Because n = 5, LOOCV trains five models.
In Fold 3, student C was removed; the model fitted on A, B, D, E predicted class 0, but the actual class was 1 — so this fold contributed a loss of 1.
Correct predictions = 4 of 5. LOOCV accuracy = 4/5 = 80%; LOOCV error rate = 1/5 = 20%.
content.title: Calculation

content.text: Mini regression example
LOOCV MAE = (1 + 2 + 1 + 3) / 4 = 1.75. Each prediction came from a model that did not train on that same observation.
content.title: Mean Absolute Error

content.text: Why LOOCV uses data efficiently
In every fold, LOOCV trains on n − 1 observations — so when n is reasonably large, each training set is almost the full dataset. This is valuable when data are scarce.

content.caption: Figure 4. Training data used in one validation split across methods — for n = 100, each LOOCV model trains on 99% of the data and validates on just 1%.

content.text: Advantages and limitations
Advantages

rows: Every model trains on all but one observation.
No random fold assignment once row membership is fixed.
Each case contributes one out-of-sample prediction.
Each model uses almost as much data as the final model.
Attractive when losing a larger validation subset is costly.

content.text: Limitations

rows: The model is trained n times — slow for large data or costly algorithms.
Training sets overlap heavily and each score uses one observation.
An outlier can produce a large loss when it is left out.
Related records can leak information across folds.
Some metrics can't be computed on one-case folds; pool predictions first.

content.text: LOOCV is not automatically the “best” method just because it uses more training data — computational cost, variance, grouping, time order, and the chosen metric all matter.
content.title: Important caution

content.text: Bias and variance intuition

LOOCV generally has low bias because each fold trains on nearly the entire dataset. But its estimate can have relatively high variance: the n training sets are extremely similar, while each validation result depends on a single observation.

rows: Training on n − 1 cases closely resembles training on all n.
A single unusual left-out case can strongly affect one fold's loss.
Two training sets differ by one observation, so models are often similar.

content.caption: Figure 5. Conceptual comparison only: LOOCV tends toward low bias but higher variance. Exact values depend on the dataset, algorithm, and metric.

content.text: Computational cost

content.caption: Figure 6. The number of model fits grows directly with dataset size for LOOCV (n fits), while k-fold stays constant — LOOCV becomes expensive as n grows.

content.text: For a model that takes 2 seconds to train, n = 10,000 would need about 20,000 seconds (≈ 5.6 hours) for one LOOCV evaluation, excluding overhead.
content.title: Practical meaning

content.text: LOOCV compared with related methods
LOOCV is exactly K-fold cross-validation with k set equal to the number of observations: k = n.
content.title: Remember

content.text: When to use — and when to avoid

content.caption: Figure 7. A simple decision guide: LOOCV can be useful when the dataset is small and the model fits quickly; otherwise prefer 5- or 10-fold CV or a faster model.

content.text: LOOCV may be suitable when:

items: The dataset is small and every training observation is valuable.
The learning algorithm is fast to train.
The data are independent and identically distributed.
You want one out-of-sample prediction for every observation.
You can pool all left-out predictions before calculating the final metric.

content.text: LOOCV should usually be avoided or modified when:

items: The dataset is large or the model is computationally expensive.
Rows are grouped, repeated, spatially related, or time-ordered.
Strong class imbalance makes single-case folds unstable.
Nested LOOCV for hyperparameter tuning would create excessive computation.
A 5-fold or 10-fold estimate is reliable enough and much faster.

content.text: Common mistakes and correct practice

rows: Preprocessing the full dataset before LOOCV
Fit scaling/imputation/selection only on the n−1 training cases in each fold.
Selecting features using all labels first
Do feature selection inside the CV pipeline to prevent leakage.
Pool all n out-of-fold predictions, then compute the metric once.
Use group-aware validation so one subject's records stay together.
For forecasting, use time-series validation instead.
Also inspect individual errors, outliers, and the residual distribution.

content.text: Anything learned from data — means, standard deviations, imputation values, selected features, model parameters — must be learned from the training portion of each fold only.
content.title: Data-leakage rule

content.text: Implementation in Python
scikit-learn's LeaveOneOut splitter with cross_val_predict gives each observation one prediction from a model that never trained on it.

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# X = feature matrix; y = class labels
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression())

loo = LeaveOneOut()
y_pred = cross_val_predict(model, X, y, cv=loo)

loocv_accuracy = accuracy_score(y, y_pred)
print(loocv_accuracy)
content.explanation: LeaveOneOut() creates n folds; the pipeline refits scaling inside each fold; cross_val_predict returns one out-of-fold prediction per observation; accuracy_score scores the pooled predictions.

content.text: Simple pseudocode

content.code:
losses = []
for i in range(n):
    training_data = all observations except i
    test_case = observation i
    model.fit(training_data)
    prediction = model.predict(test_case)
    losses.append(loss(actual_i, prediction))

loocv_error = average(losses)

content.text: Quick revision

rows: Leave one out, train on n−1, repeat n times.
Uses almost all data for training in every fold.
Requires n model fits; estimate can be high-variance.
Small datasets, fast models, independent observations.
All preprocessing inside each training fold.

content.text: Self-check

1. A dataset has 30 observations — how many LOOCV folds and model fits are required? 2. How many training and validation observations are used in each fold when n = 30? 3. Why does LOOCV usually have low bias? 4. Why can LOOCV be computationally expensive? 5. Why must standardisation be fitted separately inside each fold?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: 30 folds and 30 model fits.
29 training observations and 1 validation observation.
Each model trains on nearly the full dataset.
The model is retrained once for every observation.
Fitting on the full dataset would let information from the left-out observation influence training, causing data leakage.

keyPoints: LOOCV sets k = n: it trains n models, each leaving out one observation, then averages the n losses.
It maximises training data per fold (n − 1 observations), giving low bias — useful for very small datasets.
Its cost grows linearly with n (n model fits), and its estimate can have high variance because the folds are nearly identical.
Metrics like precision or AUC should be computed on pooled out-of-fold predictions, not per one-case fold.
Prefer 5- or 10-fold CV for large datasets or slow models, and use group- or time-aware splitters for dependent or ordered data.
commonMistakes: Fitting preprocessing on the full dataset before LOOCV instead of inside each training fold.
Computing per-fold metrics on single test cases rather than pooling all predictions first.
Using ordinary LOOCV on grouped or time-ordered data, causing leakage.
Choosing LOOCV for a large dataset or expensive model where k-fold is reliable and far faster.

lessons.title: Time-Series Validation
lessons.summary: How to evaluate models on time-ordered data without letting the future leak into training: why random splitting fails, chronological holdout, walk-forward (rolling-origin) validation, expanding vs sliding windows, safety gaps/embargoes, design choices, a monthly-sales worked example with fold construction and drift interpretation, forecasting metrics (MAE/RMSE/MAPE/sMAPE/MASE), baseline comparison, temporal leakage sources, special cases (panel data, classification, irregular timestamps, multi-step), a scikit-learn TimeSeriesSplit example, method comparison, and a full practical workflow.

content.text: Respecting the arrow of time

When data arrive in time order — sales, sensor readings, prices, patient visits — you cannot shuffle them for validation. Doing so lets the model peek at the future. Time-series validation keeps the past in training and the future in validation, so the evaluation mirrors what really happens when you forecast.

content.caption: Figure 1. A chronological split preserves the direction of time — earliest months train, later months validate, and the most recent months form the final test.

content.text: A model must be trained only on information that would have been available before the period being predicted.
content.title: Core rule

content.text: These notes stay focused on validating models when observations are ordered in time.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Explain why ordinary random train–test splitting is unsafe for time-dependent data.
Create chronological holdout, expanding-window, and sliding-window schemes.
Choose a forecast horizon, fold size, window length, and safety gap.
Evaluate models across several time folds using forecasting metrics.
Recognise and prevent temporal data leakage.
Use time-series cross-validation results to select and tune a model responsibly.

content.text: Definition

A model-evaluation procedure that respects chronological order: earlier observations train the model and later observations validate or test it, imitating real forecasting where the future is unknown when the model is fitted.

rows: Observations have a meaningful sequence (minutes, days, months).
The historical interval used to estimate model parameters.
A later interval for model selection and tuning.
The final untouched future interval, used once.
How far ahead the model must predict (e.g. 7 days, 12 months).
The latest time point available when a forecast is made.

content.text: Why random validation fails here

In random splitting, future rows can enter the training set while older rows go to the test set. The model then indirectly learns from information that would not have existed at prediction time — and the reported score is unrealistically high.

rows: Training includes rows recorded after the test row.
The score is too optimistic vs live deployment.
The evaluation misses that the process changes.

content.text: Do not use a shuffled K-fold split for forecasting unless the problem has been carefully transformed into independent groups and time dependence is genuinely irrelevant.
content.title: Incorrect practice

content.text: Basic chronological holdout
The simplest valid approach keeps the earliest observations for training and the latest for validation and testing. For a retailer with 36 months of sales forecasting the next six months:
One holdout period gives only one performance estimate — a lucky or unusually difficult period can strongly affect the result.
content.title: Limitation

content.text: Walk-forward validation

Walk-forward validation (rolling-origin evaluation) repeatedly moves the forecast origin forward. At each fold, the model is fitted on past data and evaluated on the immediately following block. It is the most common general-purpose forecasting strategy.

content.caption: Figure 2. Each fold predicts a later block using only earlier observations, with the training window growing as the origin moves forward.

content.text: Step-by-step procedure

items: Choose the minimum history needed for the first training window.
Choose the validation horizon (e.g. one week or three months).
Fit the complete preprocessing and modelling pipeline on the current training window.
Predict the next validation period.
Store the fold score and predictions.
Move the forecast origin forward and repeat.
Average the fold scores and inspect variation across folds.

content.text: Why multiple folds help

items: They test the model under several market, weather, demand, or operating conditions.
They show whether performance is stable or depends on a particular period.
They reveal deterioration caused by drift or regime changes.
They provide a stronger basis for choosing between competing models.

content.text: Expanding vs sliding window

content.caption: Figure 3. Two ways to update the training data during walk-forward validation: an expanding window keeps all history and grows, while a sliding window keeps a fixed length and drops the oldest data.

rows: Starts at the first observation and grows each fold
Old patterns may dilute recent behaviour
Keeps a fixed length, dropping the oldest observations

content.text: Decision guide

items: Use an expanding window when the process is reasonably stable and more history helps.
Use a sliding window when the process changes and old observations are no longer representative.
Compare both with the same forecast horizon when the correct choice is uncertain.

content.text: Validation with a gap (embargo)
A gap is an unused interval placed between the training and validation periods. It matters when features or labels overlap across time, or when data near the boundary are strongly dependent.

content.caption: Figure 4. A gap separates training observations from the validation target period, reducing leakage from lagged or overlapping targets.

items: Lagged features may be safe, but centred rolling statistics are not — they can include future values.
Financial labels based on future returns may overlap with neighbouring samples.
Operational data may be delayed, revised, or aggregated over intervals.
A safety gap should match the maximum overlap or information delay in the pipeline.

content.text: Important design choices

rows: How much history is needed to learn the pattern?
How far ahead will predictions be used?
How far does the origin move each fold?
Wrong choice ignores drift or history
Leakage if the gap is too short
Too few gives a noisy estimate
How often will the deployed model update?

content.text: Design the validation scheme to imitate the real production process: same data availability, same forecast horizon, and same retraining frequency.
content.title: Best practice

content.text: Worked example: monthly sales forecasting

A company has 48 months of sales data, aims to predict the next three months, and retrains every three months. The design uses an expanding window, 24-month initial training, 3-month steps, 7 folds, MAE as the metric, and the last 6 months as the final test.
Fold construction
Example fold results

content.caption: Figure 5. Validation error across time folds (mean MAE ≈ 9.35). Average error alone is not enough — the final fold is worse, hinting at drift.

content.text: The mean MAE is about 9.35, but the final fold is worse than earlier ones, suggesting the process may be changing. Compare a recent-data sliding window or a drift-aware retraining policy before deployment.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Evaluation metrics

rows: Easy to interpret in original units

content.text: Use the metric that reflects the real business cost — RMSE when large misses are especially damaging, MAE when interpretability matters most.
content.title: Metric rule

content.text: Always compare with a baseline
A complex model should beat a simple forecast that needs no machine learning.

rows: Next value = value from the same prior season
Next value = mean of recent observations

content.text: Temporal data leakage
When the model, preprocessing, or feature engineering uses information from the future relative to the prediction time — inflating validation and test scores.

rows: Fit StandardScaler on the whole dataset
Fit the scaler inside each training fold only
Use a global mean including future rows
Estimate imputation from the training fold
Use a trailing average shifted before the target
Run selection only on each training fold
Tune repeatedly on the final test period
Tune on validation folds; use test once

content.text: Every learned transformation — scaling, imputation, encoding, feature selection, dimensionality reduction — must be fitted separately inside each training fold.
content.title: Pipeline principle

content.text: Special situations
Multiple related series (panel data)

items: Split by time across all entities so future dates do not enter training.
Consider a second evaluation on unseen entities when generalisation to new stores/patients/machines matters.
Group-aware and time-aware restrictions may need to be combined.

content.text: Classification with time order

Time-series validation is also needed when the target is categorical — fraud next hour, equipment failure next day, churn next month. Use time-ordered folds and classification metrics (precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC).
Irregular timestamps

items: Prefer splitting by timestamp boundaries rather than by row count.
Check whether some periods contain unusually many observations.
Match the validation horizon to real elapsed time, not a fixed number of rows.

content.text: Multi-step forecasting
Evaluate exactly the horizons used in practice. A model may be accurate one step ahead but poor twelve steps ahead — report error by horizon as well as the overall average.
Python example (scikit-learn)
TimeSeriesSplit produces time-ordered folds; the pipeline keeps the scaler fitted only on each training fold.

content.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, cross_validate
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

# X and y are sorted from oldest to newest.
tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, test_size=12, gap=2)

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge(alpha=1.0))

scores = cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=tscv, scoring={
    "mae": "neg_mean_absolute_error",
    "rmse": "neg_root_mean_squared_error"
})

print(-scores["test_mae"].mean(), -scores["test_rmse"].mean())
content.explanation: test_size sets the validation horizon and gap adds an embargo. TimeSeriesSplit is a splitter, not a full forecasting system — lag construction, target alignment, and deployment timing must still be handled correctly.

content.text: Comparison with other methods
Advantages and limitations

rows: Computationally expensive — models retrained many times
Fewer usable folds when the series is short
Results depend on horizon, window, and fold design
Strong non-stationarity makes old folds less relevant
Overlapping labels may require purging or gaps

content.text: Recommended workflow

items: Sort by timestamp and remove duplicate or inconsistent timestamps.
Define the real prediction time, target horizon, and retraining schedule.
Reserve the latest period as a final untouched test set.
Construct walk-forward folds on the remaining development data.
Build lagged and rolling features using only past observations.
Fit every preprocessing step inside each training fold.
Compare against naïve and seasonal-naïve baselines.
Report mean, median, spread, worst-fold error, and error by horizon.
Select the model and hyperparameters using validation folds only.
Refit on all pre-test data and evaluate once on the final test set.
After deployment, monitor drift and re-evaluate when the environment changes.

content.text: Validation checklist

items: Are observations sorted from oldest to newest?
Does every training fold end before its validation fold begins?
Does the validation horizon match the real prediction horizon?
Are all transformations fitted only on training data?
Are lagged and rolling features shifted correctly?
Is a gap required because labels or features overlap?
Is the final test period untouched?
Is performance compared with a suitable baseline?
Are fold-to-fold variation and worst-case periods reported?
Does the validation design imitate deployment and retraining?

content.text: Common mistakes to avoid

items: Shuffling before splitting.
Using a forecast horizon easier than the real business horizon.
Creating rolling features before splitting without checking future leakage.
Tuning on the final test period.
Reporting only the average score and hiding unstable folds.
Ignoring a naïve or seasonal-naïve baseline.
Using too little history to represent seasonality.
Keeping very old data when strong concept drift makes it irrelevant.
Evaluating one-step predictions when deployment requires multi-step forecasts.

content.text: Key summary

items: Time-series validation keeps the past in training and the future in validation.
Walk-forward validation provides several realistic forecasting experiments.
Expanding windows retain all history; sliding windows focus on recent history.
A gap is useful when samples, labels, or engineered features overlap in time.
All preprocessing must be fitted inside each training fold.
The final test set is used only once, after model selection.
A reliable report includes baseline comparison, fold variation, and errors by horizon.

content.text: Quick self-check

1. Why is random K-fold usually unsuitable for time-series forecasting? 2. What is the main difference between expanding and sliding windows? 3. Why might a gap be needed? 4. When should the final test set be used? 5. What should a validation scheme imitate?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: It can train on future observations and breaks the chronological dependence.
The expanding window keeps all earlier data; the sliding window drops older observations to keep a fixed length.
To prevent leakage from overlapping labels, delayed data, or strongly dependent boundary observations.
Only once, after all modelling and tuning decisions are complete.
The real deployment horizon, data availability, and retraining schedule.

keyPoints: Time-series validation trains on the past and validates on the future, imitating real forecasting — never shuffle time-ordered data.
Walk-forward (rolling-origin) validation runs several realistic forecasts; expanding windows keep all history while sliding windows focus on recent data.
A safety gap (embargo) between training and validation prevents leakage from overlapping labels or delayed data.
Fit every preprocessing step inside each training fold, build lag/rolling features from past data only, and use the test period once.
Report more than the mean: fold-to-fold variation, worst-fold error, error by horizon, and a comparison against naïve/seasonal-naïve baselines.
commonMistakes: Shuffling before splitting, or using a random K-fold on forecasting data.
Computing scaling, imputation, or rolling/centred features on the full series, causing temporal leakage.
Evaluating an easier horizon than deployment needs, or only one-step when multi-step is required.
Reporting only the average score while hiding unstable folds, and ignoring a naïve baseline.

lessons.title: Regression Metrics
lessons.summary: The numerical measures that judge how close a regression model's predictions are to the true continuous values. Covers key terms and residuals, a five-row worked example, the core metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, R-squared, Adjusted R-squared) and percentage/robust metrics (MAPE, Median AE, MSLE/RMSLE) with formulas, interpretations, and strengths/limitations, residual analysis, a full comparison table, a decision guide for choosing a metric, common mistakes, and a scikit-learn example.

content.text: Turning errors into scores

Once a regression model makes predictions, you need a number that says how good they are. Regression metrics turn the gaps between predicted and actual values into scores you can compare across models, features, and experiments — and each metric emphasises a different aspect of those errors.

content.caption: Figure 1. The vertical distance between each actual and predicted value is the prediction error — the raw material every regression metric summarises.

content.text: A regression model is not judged only by whether predictions look close. A metric summarises the size, pattern, or explained variation of the prediction errors.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on regression evaluation metrics. Classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC, log loss) are covered separately.
content.title: Scope

content.text: Key terms

rows: The value estimated by the model.
Actual minus predicted: e = y − ŷ.
A loss is optimised during training; a metric reports performance (sometimes the same formula).
MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE, MSLE, Median AE.

content.text: Worked example dataset
Five observations demonstrate every metric below. The residual is actual minus predicted:

Positive and negative residuals can cancel (their sum here is −1.0), producing a misleading average near zero. That is why useful metrics apply an absolute value, a square, or another transformation before averaging.
content.title: Important

content.text: Core regression metrics
Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
The average of the absolute differences between actual and predicted values.

content.explanation: Expressed in the same unit as the target; lower means predictions are closer to actual values.

rows: Easy to explain; same unit as the target; less affected by extreme errors than MSE/RMSE.
Treats every error linearly; does not strongly punish a few very large mistakes.
Each unit of error has roughly equal cost and interpretability matters.

content.text: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
The average of squared prediction errors.

content.explanation: Smaller is better; because errors are squared, a large error contributes far more than a small one.

content.caption: Figure 2. Squaring causes a single large error to dominate MSE and RMSE — an error of 12 contributes vastly more than several small errors combined.

rows: Strongly penalises large mistakes; smooth and widely used as a training loss.
Measured in squared units, so hard to explain directly; highly sensitive to outliers.
Large errors are especially costly, or the algorithm optimises squared error.

content.text: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
The square root of MSE, returning the error to the original target unit.

content.explanation: Usually greater than or equal to MAE; keeps the large-error penalty but in the target's own unit.

content.text: Mini example: RMSE = √1.10 = 1.05.

rows: Same unit as the target; extra weight on large errors; common in forecasting benchmarks.
Sensitive to outliers; a few extreme mistakes can make a model look poor.
Large mistakes must be penalised, but the score still needs target units.

content.text: If RMSE is much larger than MAE, the model probably has some large errors. If the two are close, the errors are more consistent.
content.title: MAE vs RMSE

content.text: R-squared (coefficient of determination)
How much of the variation in the target the model explains, compared with predicting the target mean for every observation.

content.explanation: R² = 1 is perfect; R² = 0 is no better than the mean-only baseline; a negative value is worse than that baseline.

content.caption: Figure 3. R-squared measures how much better the model is than simply predicting the target mean (the dashed baseline).

rows: Unit-free; useful for relative fit; commonly reported in statistical regression.
Hides real error size; can rise after adding weak predictors; high R² doesn't prove good predictions everywhere.
You need a goodness-of-fit measure versus a mean-only baseline.

content.text: Adjusted R-squared
R-squared modified to account for the number of predictors and observations.

content.explanation: It rises only when a new predictor improves the model enough to justify the added complexity (p = number of predictors).

content.text: Mini example: with n = 5, p = 1, and R² = 0.788, adjusted R² ≈ 0.718. (This tiny dataset is only for calculation practice.)

rows: Better than plain R² for comparing linear models with different numbers of predictors.
Still hides error magnitude; unstable in tiny samples; not a substitute for validation on unseen data.
Comparing multiple linear-regression models that use different numbers of inputs.

content.text: Results from the example

rows: Predictions are off by 0.80 target units on average.
Average squared error is 1.10 squared units.
Typical error ≈ 1.05 units, with extra penalty on large errors.
Explains about 78.8% of the variation in this small example.
R-squared adjusted for one predictor and the tiny sample.
Average absolute percentage error is about 13.19%.
Half the absolute errors are 0.50 units or less.

content.text: Percentage and robust metrics
Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)
The average absolute error expressed as a percentage of the actual value.

content.explanation: A MAPE of 10% means predictions differ from actual values by about 10% on average.

content.text: Mini example: MAPE ≈ 13.19% for the sample data.

rows: Undefined at zero; unstable near zero; can penalise over- and under-prediction unevenly.
Actual values are strictly positive and safely away from zero.

content.text: Do not use ordinary MAPE when the target contains zeros or very small values. Consider MAE, RMSE, WAPE, sMAPE, or a domain-specific metric instead.
content.title: MAPE warning

content.text: Median Absolute Error
The median of the absolute prediction errors — half the predictions have an absolute error at or below this value.
Mini example: absolute errors are [0.5, 0.5, 0, 1, 2], so Median AE = 0.50.

rows: Very robust to outliers; useful when a few extremes shouldn't control the score.
May hide serious tail errors; less sensitive to general improvement than the mean.
The error distribution has outliers and the typical case matters most.

content.text: MSLE and RMSLE
Squared error computed after applying log(1 + value) to actual and predicted values (RMSLE is its square root).

content.explanation: Emphasises relative differences — predicting 20 instead of 10 is treated similarly to predicting 200 instead of 100.

rows: Good for targets spanning several orders of magnitude; reduces the effect of very large values.
Requires non-negative values; unsuitable when absolute errors are the real business cost.
Targets are non-negative, highly skewed, and proportional accuracy matters (counts, some prices).

content.text: Use MSLE/RMSLE only after confirming that negative target values are impossible or have been handled appropriately.
content.title: Requirement

content.text: Residual analysis: metrics are not enough
A single score can hide systematic problems. Residual plots reveal whether errors look random or follow a pattern.

content.caption: Figure 4. A residual plot should ideally show a random cloud around zero — structure signals a missing pattern or changing error variance.

rows: The model form may be reasonably appropriate.
The relationship may be nonlinear or features are missing.
Error variance changes with prediction level (heteroscedasticity).
Important groups or data-collection effects may be unmodelled.
Possible outliers, data errors, or rare cases to investigate.
The model systematically under- or over-predicts.

content.text: Comparing regression metrics

rows: Hard to interpret in real units
Does not show real error size
Fails at zero; unstable near zero

content.caption: Figure 5. Model rankings can change with the metric: Model B has the lowest MAE (2.9) but the highest RMSE (5.8), because it makes a few large errors.

content.text: How to choose the right metric

content.caption: Figure 6. A practical decision guide: pick a metric by whether you need original units, large-error penalties, explained variation, or percentage/proportional error — and always inspect residuals.

items: Use at least one metric in the original unit — usually MAE or RMSE.
Use RMSE or MSE when large mistakes are especially harmful.
Use MAE when every unit of error has similar cost and a clear explanation is needed.
Use R-squared or Adjusted R-squared as supporting goodness-of-fit measures, not the only evaluation.
Use MAPE only after checking for zero and near-zero actual values.
Compare all models on the same untouched validation or test set.
Choose the final metric by the real-world cost of errors, not just because it is popular.

content.text: Common mistakes and correct practice

rows: Also report an error metric (MAE or RMSE) in the target unit.
Use the same split, preprocessing, and target definition.
Choose a zero-safe alternative or redesign the percentage metric.
MAE/RMSE are meaningful only relative to the target unit and range.
Repeatedly selecting on the test set
Use validation/CV for selection; reserve the test set for final evaluation.
Investigate whether outliers are genuine, data errors, or a separate population.
Compare against baselines and check business/scientific relevance.
Report CV mean and standard deviation or confidence intervals.

content.text: Python example

content.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import (
    mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error,
    r2_score, mean_absolute_percentage_error,
    median_absolute_error
)

y_true = np.array([3, 5, 2, 7, 8])
y_pred = np.array([2.5, 5.5, 2, 6, 10])

mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
mse = mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)
rmse = np.sqrt(mse)
r2 = r2_score(y_true, y_pred)
mape = mean_absolute_percentage_error(y_true, y_pred) * 100
medae = median_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)

print(mae, mse, rmse, r2, mape, medae)
content.explanation: Reproduces the worked example: MAE 0.80, MSE 1.10, RMSE 1.05, R² 0.788, MAPE ≈ 13.19%, Median AE 0.50.

content.text: Quick revision

rows: Average absolute error; easy to interpret; original unit.
Average squared error; strongly penalises large mistakes.
Square root of MSE; large-error penalty in original unit.
Proportion of target variation explained vs a mean baseline.
R-squared corrected for model size and sample size.
Average percentage error; avoid with zero/near-zero actuals.
Log-scale metric for non-negative, highly skewed targets.

content.text: For each metric, state its formula, direction (lower or higher is better), unit, sensitivity to outliers, and one suitable use case.
content.title: Exam tip

content.text: Self-check

1. Why can positive and negative residuals not simply be averaged? 2. When would RMSE be preferred over MAE? 3. Why can R-squared be negative on test data? 4. What problem occurs when MAPE is used with an actual value of zero? 5. What does a funnel shape in a residual plot suggest? 6. Why should a final regression report include more than one metric?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answer key

items: They can cancel out, giving a misleading average near zero even when predictions are inaccurate.
When large errors should receive a stronger penalty than small ones.
When the model predicts worse than simply using the test-set target mean as a baseline.
MAPE divides by the actual value, so a zero makes it undefined; near-zero values give huge percentages.
Non-constant error variance (heteroscedasticity).
Different metrics reveal different properties — a strong report combines real-unit error, large-error sensitivity, fit, and residual inspection.

keyPoints: Regression metrics turn residuals into comparable scores; MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE, MSLE, and Median AE are lower-is-better, while R-squared and Adjusted R-squared are higher-is-better.
MAE reports average error in the target unit; MSE/RMSE add a strong penalty for large errors (RMSE stays in target units).
R-squared measures explained variation versus a mean-only baseline and can go negative on test data; Adjusted R-squared accounts for the number of predictors.
MAPE is intuitive but breaks at or near zero; Median AE is robust to outliers; MSLE/RMSLE suit non-negative, highly skewed targets.
No single score is enough — report a real-unit error plus a fit measure, inspect residual plots, and choose the metric by the real cost of errors.
commonMistakes: Averaging raw residuals, letting positive and negative errors cancel.
Reporting only R-squared without an error metric in the target unit.
Using MAPE when the target contains zeros or near-zero values.
Comparing metrics computed on different data splits or preprocessing, or picking a model repeatedly on the test set.

lessons.title: Classification Metrics
lessons.summary: The measures that judge how well a classifier assigns discrete classes, built from the confusion matrix. Covers TP/TN/FP/FN, accuracy and error rate, precision, recall, specificity, FPR/FNR, F1 and F-beta, balanced accuracy, and MCC (with a 100-patient worked example), the accuracy trap under class imbalance, decision thresholds and the precision-recall trade-off, ROC/ROC-AUC and PR/PR-AUC, probability metrics (log loss, Brier, calibration), multiclass averaging (macro/micro/weighted/per-class), multilabel metrics, a choose-the-metric guide, common mistakes, and a full worked calculation.

content.text: Judging classifiers

A classifier that is “correct 90% of the time” can still be useless — if 90% of cases are negative, predicting “negative” always scores 90% while catching zero positives. Classification metrics look past raw correctness to answer the questions that actually matter: how many alarms are false, how many real cases are missed, and how well the model ranks its predictions.
A classifier is not “good” simply because it is correct often. The right metric depends on the cost of false positives, false negatives, class imbalance, and the decision threshold.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on metrics used to evaluate classification models.
content.title: Scope

content.text: Why several metrics are needed

items: Accuracy: how often is the model correct overall?
Precision: when it predicts positive, how often is it right?
Recall: of all actual positives, how many did it find?
Specificity: of all actual negatives, how many did it reject correctly?
F1-score: summarises precision and recall in one value.
ROC-AUC and PR-AUC: evaluate ranking performance across many thresholds.

content.text: The confusion matrix: the foundation
A confusion matrix organises binary results into four outcomes. Nearly every common metric is calculated from these four counts.

Always identify the positive class first. In fraud detection “fraud” is positive; in disease screening “disease present” is positive. Reversing the positive class changes precision, recall, and related metrics.
content.title: Important

content.text: Worked example data
A medical screening model classifies 100 patients:

items: TP = 35 — patients with the condition were detected.
TN = 50 — healthy patients were correctly classified.
FP = 5 — healthy patients received a false alarm.
FN = 10 — patients with the condition were missed.

content.caption: Figure 1. The binary confusion matrix used throughout the worked example: TP = 35, TN = 50, FP = 5, FN = 10.

content.text: Core classification metrics
Accuracy and error rate

content.explanation: Worked value: (35 + 50) / 100 = 0.85 = 85%. Useful when classes are balanced and error costs are similar, but misleading on imbalanced data.

content.text: Precision (positive predictive value)

content.explanation: Worked value: 35 / (35 + 5) = 0.875 = 87.5%. High precision means few false positives.

content.text: Prioritise precision when false alarms are costly — blocking legitimate financial transactions or marking genuine email as spam.
Recall (sensitivity / true positive rate)

content.explanation: Worked value: 35 / (35 + 10) = 0.778 = 77.8%. High recall means few false negatives.

content.text: Prioritise recall when missing a positive case is dangerous — disease screening or fire detection.
Specificity (true negative rate)

content.explanation: Worked value: 50 / (50 + 5) = 0.909 = 90.9%. Recall focuses on the positive class; specificity on the negative class.

content.text: False positive and false negative rates

content.expression: FPR = FP / (FP + TN) = 1 − Specificity   |   FNR = FN / (FN + TP) = 1 − Recall
content.explanation: Worked values: FPR = 5/55 = 9.1%; FNR = 10/45 = 22.2%.

content.text: F1-score

content.explanation: Worked value: 2 × (0.875 × 0.778) / (0.875 + 0.778) = 0.824 = 82.4%. The harmonic mean penalises extreme imbalance between precision and recall.

content.text: F1 does not include true negatives, so it should not be used alone when performance on negatives matters strongly.
content.title: Caution

content.text: F-beta score

content.explanation: β = 1 gives F1 (equal emphasis); β > 1 (e.g. F2) emphasises recall; β < 1 (e.g. F0.5) emphasises precision.

content.text: Balanced accuracy

content.explanation: Worked value: (0.778 + 0.909) / 2 = 0.843 = 84.3%. More informative than ordinary accuracy when classes are imbalanced.

content.text: Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)

content.explanation: Uses all four cells; −1 = total disagreement, 0 = random, +1 = perfect. Worked value ≈ 0.69. Robust for imbalanced binary tasks but harder to interpret directly.

content.text: Comparing the metrics on one example

rows: Overall quality using all four cells

content.caption: Figure 2. The same 100 predictions score differently on each metric (77.8%–90.9%) — each describes a different aspect of performance.

content.text: Class imbalance and the accuracy trap
Class imbalance occurs when one class is far more common than another. A model can then score high accuracy by mostly predicting the majority class while failing on the minority class.

content.caption: Figure 3. A highly imbalanced dataset: 950 negatives and only 50 positives — predicting “negative” always would score 95% accuracy yet detect no positives.

content.text: A model that predicts “negative” for all 1,000 cases obtains 95% accuracy, but its recall for the positive class is 0% — it detects none of the important positive cases.
content.title: Accuracy trap

content.text: Better choices for imbalanced classes

items: Report the full confusion matrix, not accuracy alone.
Use precision, recall, F1, F-beta, balanced accuracy, or MCC.
Use a precision-recall curve when the positive class is rare.
Show per-class scores for multiclass problems.

content.text: Classification thresholds

Many classifiers output a probability or score rather than a final class. A threshold converts that score into a label — with a default of 0.50, scores at or above 0.50 become positive. Moving the threshold trades precision against recall.

content.caption: Figure 4. As the threshold rises, recall falls and precision rises; F1 peaks somewhere in between. The best threshold depends on the cost of each error type.

content.text: A lower threshold suits screening / early warning; a higher threshold suits strong confirmation before a costly action.
Choose the threshold using validation data and the real cost of errors — do not tune it on the final test set.
content.title: Best practice

content.text: ROC curve and ROC-AUC
The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate at many thresholds.

content.caption: Figure 5. An ROC curve (AUC ≈ 0.88): points closer to the top-left corner are better, and the diagonal is a random classifier.

items: ROC-AUC is the area under the ROC curve.
AUC = 1.0 indicates perfect ranking in the evaluated sample.
AUC = 0.5 indicates random-like ranking.
AUC below 0.5 may indicate reversed scores or very poor ranking.
ROC-AUC is threshold-independent, but it does not select an operating threshold.

content.text: ROC-AUC can look optimistic on highly imbalanced data because the many true negatives keep the false positive rate small. For rare-positive tasks, also examine the precision-recall curve.
content.title: Limitation

content.text: Precision-recall curve and PR-AUC
A precision-recall (PR) curve plots precision against recall over many thresholds. It focuses directly on the positive class and is especially useful when positive cases are rare.

content.caption: Figure 6. A precision-recall curve with a 20% prevalence baseline — a strong curve stays high and to the right, well above the baseline.

items: A strong curve stays close to the upper-right region.
The baseline precision is approximately the positive-class prevalence.
Average Precision (AP) is a common summary of the PR curve.
PR-AUC depends more strongly on class prevalence than ROC-AUC, so compare only similarly distributed datasets.

content.text: Metrics for predicted probabilities
Label-based metrics evaluate final class decisions. Probability-based metrics evaluate whether the predicted probabilities themselves are accurate and well calibrated.

rows: Penalises incorrect probabilities; confident wrong predictions cost a lot.
Mean squared difference between predicted probability and actual outcome.
Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies.
Of cases predicted ~0.70, about 70% should be positive.

content.expression: Log loss = −(1/N) Σ [y log(p) + (1−y) log(1−p)]   |   Brier = (1/N) Σ (p − y)²
content.explanation: p is the predicted probability, y is 0 or 1. A confident correct prediction gives low loss; a confident wrong one gives high loss.

content.text: A model can rank cases well (high AUC) but still produce poorly calibrated probabilities — ranking and calibration are different properties.
content.title: Key distinction

content.text: Multiclass classification metrics
In multiclass problems, precision, recall, and F1 are computed per class using a one-vs-rest view, then combined by averaging.

rows: Metric per class, then unweighted mean
Treats every class equally; highlights weak minorities
Pool all TP, FP, FN before computing
Favours common classes; equals accuracy for single-label multiclass
Reflects frequency; may hide poor rare-class performance
Most transparent; essential when classes differ in importance

content.text: Example: class-wise F1 of A = 0.90, B = 0.75, C = 0.45 gives macro F1 = (0.90 + 0.75 + 0.45)/3 = 0.70 — immediately showing the weakest class lowers the result.
content.title: Macro example

content.text: For multiclass datasets, report the confusion matrix, per-class precision/recall/F1, macro average, weighted average, and the support (count) of each class.
content.title: Reporting recommendation

content.text: Multilabel classification metrics
In multilabel classification, one observation can carry several correct labels at once (an image may contain both “car” and “person”), so ordinary accuracy must be interpreted carefully.

rows: Correct only when the full predicted label set matches the true set.
Fraction of individual label assignments that are wrong.
Intersection over union of predicted and true label sets.
Combines multilabel TP/FP/FN globally or per label.

content.text: Choosing the right metric

rows: Missing a true case is costly.
Catch fraud without blocking valid transactions.
Probability quality matters, not just ranking.
Evaluate ordering before choosing a threshold.

content.text: Common mistakes and good practice

rows: Also report the confusion matrix and class-sensitive metrics.
State clearly which class is positive.
Selecting a threshold on test data
Tune on validation; evaluate once on untouched test data.
Comparing AUC across very different distributions
Check prevalence, sampling, and evaluation protocol.
Add macro and per-class scores to reveal minority performance.
Choose the threshold from costs, constraints, and validation.
Use cross-validation or bootstrapping to show uncertainty.
Compute each fold consistently; report mean with spread.

content.text: Complete worked calculation
Given TP = 35, TN = 50, FP = 5, FN = 10:
Cheat sheet

There is no single “best” classification metric. The correct choice follows from class distribution, the cost of false positives and false negatives, whether probabilities are used, and whether a fixed threshold or ranking performance is being evaluated.
content.title: Final takeaway

content.text: Self-check

1. Why can a model reach 95% accuracy yet be useless on a rare positive class? 2. When should recall be prioritised over precision? 3. Why must the positive class be defined before computing precision/recall? 4. Why can ROC-AUC look optimistic on imbalanced data? 5. What is the difference between good ranking and good calibration? 6. For a multiclass problem with rare classes, which averages should you report?
content.title: Test yourself

keyPoints: Nearly all binary metrics come from the confusion matrix (TP, TN, FP, FN) — and the positive class must be defined first.
Accuracy is misleading under imbalance; use precision, recall, F1, balanced accuracy, MCC, or PR-AUC instead.
Precision vs recall is a threshold trade-off: prioritise recall when misses are dangerous, precision when false alarms are costly; tune the threshold on validation data.
ROC-AUC measures threshold-independent ranking but can look optimistic on rare-positive data, where the PR curve is more informative.
Probability metrics (log loss, Brier, calibration) evaluate probability quality — a model can rank well yet be poorly calibrated; for multiclass, report per-class plus macro/weighted averages.
commonMistakes: Reporting accuracy alone on imbalanced data and hiding zero minority-class recall.
Failing to state which class is positive, changing precision/recall.
Tuning the decision threshold on the test set instead of validation.
Comparing AUC values across datasets with very different class prevalence.

lessons.title: Confusion Matrix Interpretation
lessons.summary: How to read and reason about a confusion matrix rather than just a single score. Covers the binary structure (TP/TN/FP/FN) and axis orientation, a five-step interpretation sequence, a 100-person medical worked example with derived metrics, the false-positive-vs-false-negative cost question across applications, the accuracy trap under class imbalance, how the decision threshold reshapes the matrix, multiclass matrices (diagonal and off-diagonal confusions), raw vs normalized matrices, common mistakes, an interpretation checklist, and a spam-classifier practice set.

content.text: Reading the matrix, not just the score

A confusion matrix is the most honest summary of a classifier's behaviour: it shows not only how many predictions were right, but the type of each correct prediction and the direction of each error. Learning to read it — diagonal, off-diagonal, and the cost behind each cell — is what separates a real evaluation from a single misleading number.
The matrix does not only show how many predictions were correct. It shows the type of each correct prediction and the direction of each error.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on how to read, explain, and use a confusion matrix for classification model evaluation.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define a confusion matrix and explain why it is used.
Identify true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.
Interpret a binary matrix using counts, rates, and error costs.
Calculate accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, and F1-score from matrix values.
Read multiclass and normalized confusion matrices.
Recognise misleading interpretations, especially with imbalanced data.

content.text: Definition and structure
A table that compares a classification model's predicted labels with the actual labels, summarising correct predictions and classification errors for each class.

content.caption: Figure 1. In a binary confusion matrix, rows are the actual classes and columns are the predictions — always verify this orientation, because some software reverses it.

content.text: How to interpret a confusion matrix

content.caption: Figure 2. A reliable five-step sequence: check class order → read the diagonal → inspect FP/FN → calculate metrics → judge business cost.

items: Confirm class order and axis orientation — which class is positive, and whether rows are actual or predicted.
Read the diagonal first — diagonal cells are correct predictions; larger values usually mean better classification.
Inspect off-diagonal cells — these are errors (FP and FN in binary classification).
Convert counts into rates — precision, recall, and specificity enable fairer comparison than raw counts.
Interpret errors in context — the same accuracy can have very different consequences depending on whether FP or FN is costlier.

content.text: Worked binary example
A medical screening model evaluates 100 people, where the positive class is “disease present.”

content.caption: Figure 3. The worked-example matrix: TP = 45, FN = 5, FP = 8, TN = 42 — 87 correct predictions and 13 errors.

rows: 8 healthy people received a false positive.

content.text: The model performs well overall, but the five false negatives deserve special attention in medical screening — a missed disease case may be far more harmful than a false alarm.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Metrics derived from the matrix
The matrix is the source for several metrics, each answering a different question:

content.explanation: What proportion of all predictions was correct?
When the model predicts positive, how often is it correct?
Of all actual positives, how many did the model find?
Of all actual negatives, how many did the model reject correctly?
The harmonic balance between precision and recall.

content.expression: FPR = FP / (FP + TN)   |   FNR = FN / (FN + TP)
content.explanation: The share of actual negatives that became false alarms, and of actual positives that were missed.

content.text: Calculations for the worked example

content.caption: Figure 4. Different metrics emphasise different cells (84.0%–90.0% here), so one metric should not replace full matrix interpretation.

content.text: False positives vs false negatives
The most important interpretation question is often not “How many errors?” but “Which error is more costly?”

rows: A legitimate email goes to spam
Both matter; FN causes direct loss
A real fire is not detected

content.text: The “best” model depends on the cost of FP and FN. The same confusion matrix may be acceptable in one application and unacceptable in another.
content.title: Key principle

content.text: Class imbalance and misleading accuracy
Accuracy can look high when one class is much more common. Consider 1,000 transactions with only 20 fraud cases, where the model predicts “normal” for everything:
Accuracy = 980 / 1,000 = 98%, but recall for fraud = 0 / 20 = 0%. The model completely fails to detect the minority class.
content.title: Accuracy trap

content.text: For imbalanced datasets, inspect class-wise recall, precision, F1-score, balanced accuracy, and the full confusion matrix rather than reporting accuracy alone.
content.title: Interpret carefully

content.text: Decision threshold and matrix changes
Many classifiers output probabilities. A decision threshold converts a probability into a label — and changing it changes TP, TN, FP, and FN.

content.caption: Figure 5. Lowering the threshold finds more positives (recall 96% at 0.3) but adds false alarms (precision 70%); raising it reverses the trade-off (recall 62%, precision 96% at 0.7).

content.text: Multiclass confusion matrix
For more than two classes, each row is one actual class and each column one predicted class. Every class can be analysed as “one class versus all others.”

content.caption: Figure 6. A Cat/Dog/Bird matrix — the model is strongest on Cat and Bird (46 each); Dog is most often confused with Bird (7 cases).

items: Diagonal cells show correct predictions per class: Cat = 46, Dog = 38, Bird = 46.
Row-wise reading answers: “For this actual class, what did the model predict?”
Column-wise reading answers: “Which actual classes were assigned this predicted label?”
The cell Actual Dog → Predicted Bird = 7 identifies a specific confusion pattern.
Class-wise recall comes from a row; class-wise precision comes from a column.

content.text: Raw counts vs normalized matrices

rows: Number of observations in each cell
Shows real volume of correct/incorrect predictions
Can hide poor performance on a small class
Makes class-wise recall and confusion easy to compare
Does not show the actual sample size
Helps interpret prediction purity / class-wise precision

content.text: Common interpretation mistakes

rows: Libraries may place actual on rows or columns.
TP and FP change meaning when it changes.
State clearly which label is positive.
It can hide failure on a minority class.
Report class-wise metrics and error counts.
A larger test set produces larger counts.
Use normalized rates when sizes differ.
Treating FP and FN as equal

content.text: Interpretation checklist

items: Identify the positive class.
Confirm whether rows are actual labels and columns are predicted labels.
Report TP, TN, FP, and FN using both numbers and plain language.
Calculate metrics that match the task objective.
Compare FP and FN costs.
Check minority-class performance and class imbalance.
Inspect specific multiclass confusions.
Use a validation or test set.
Consider whether the decision threshold should change.
Explain the result in the application context.

content.text: Quick practice
A spam classifier produced: TP = 70, TN = 110, FP = 20, FN = 10 (spam is the positive class).

items: How many emails were classified correctly?
How many legitimate emails were incorrectly sent to spam?
How many spam emails were missed?
Calculate accuracy, precision, recall, and specificity.
Which error is likely more frustrating to users: FP or FN? Explain.

content.text: Practice answers

items: Correct predictions = TP + TN = 70 + 110 = 180.
Legitimate emails sent to spam = FP = 20.
Spam emails missed = FN = 10.
FP is often more frustrating — a legitimate message may be hidden in the spam folder — though the application owner must decide the real cost.

content.text: Key takeaways

items: A confusion matrix explains both correct predictions and error types.
TP and TN are correct; FP and FN are incorrect.
Precision focuses on predicted positives; recall focuses on actual positives.
The most important error depends on the real-world cost of FP and FN.
Accuracy can be misleading for imbalanced data.
In multiclass tasks, inspect both the diagonal and specific off-diagonal confusions.
Always state the class order, axis orientation, dataset split, and decision threshold.

content.text: Self-check

1. Why must you confirm axis orientation before labelling TP, TN, FP, FN? 2. In the worked example, why do the five false negatives matter most? 3. How can 98% accuracy still mean a useless fraud detector? 4. What happens to recall and precision when the threshold is lowered? 5. In a multiclass matrix, how do you read class-wise recall vs precision?
content.title: Test yourself

keyPoints: A confusion matrix shows the type of each correct prediction and the direction of each error — read the diagonal, then the off-diagonal cells.
Always confirm axis orientation and which class is positive before labelling TP, TN, FP, and FN.
Convert counts to rates (precision, recall, specificity) for fair comparison, and judge FP vs FN by their real-world cost.
Accuracy can hide complete failure on a minority class — inspect class-wise metrics and the full matrix under imbalance.
The decision threshold reshapes the matrix (recall vs precision), and multiclass matrices reveal specific class-to-class confusions on the off-diagonal.
commonMistakes: Assuming the axis orientation instead of reading the labels, mislabelling TP/FP/FN.
Reporting accuracy alone on imbalanced data and missing zero minority-class recall.
Treating false positives and false negatives as equally costly.
Reading only the diagonal and missing specific off-diagonal confusion patterns.

lessons.title: ROC and AUC
lessons.summary: How the ROC curve and AUC evaluate a binary classifier's ranking ability across all thresholds. Covers the TPR/FPR axes, how the threshold reshapes predictions and the confusion matrix, a ten-observation worked ROC construction and AUC = 0.68 calculation (trapezoidal and pairwise-ranking), the AUC interpretation scale and probability meaning, comparing classifiers with ROC curves, choosing an operating threshold (Youden's J, cost- and constraint-based), advantages, limitations and mistakes, a comparison with related metrics, a practical workflow, and a scikit-learn example.

content.text: Judging a model across every threshold

Most classifiers output a score, and a threshold turns that score into a class. Every choice of threshold gives a different confusion matrix — so which one do you judge? ROC and AUC sidestep the question: they evaluate how well the model ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds at once, giving a single, threshold-independent picture of its discrimination ability.

content.caption: Figure 1. From probability scores to the ROC curve and AUC: change the threshold, calculate TPR and FPR, plot the curve, and measure the area under it.

content.text: Understand how ROC and AUC evaluate the ranking ability of a binary classifier across all classification thresholds.
content.title: Learning goal

content.text: These notes focus only on ROC curves and AUC — the threshold trade-off, interpretation, calculation, strengths, and limitations.
content.title: Scope

content.text: Core idea

Many models output a score or probability instead of a final class. A threshold converts that score into a predicted class, and changing the threshold changes the numbers of true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives.
A graph showing the True Positive Rate against the False Positive Rate at many classification thresholds.
The area under the ROC curve — it summarises how well the model ranks positive examples above negative examples.
Prerequisite terms

rows: The event or class of interest.
Patient does not have the disease.
Cut-off converting a score into a class.

content.text: The two ROC axes

content.expression: TPR = TP / (TP + FN)   |   FPR = FP / (FP + TN)
content.explanation: TPR (sensitivity / recall) is the share of actual positives detected; FPR is the share of actual negatives wrongly flagged positive.

items: The ROC curve plots FPR on the horizontal axis and TPR on the vertical axis.
A desirable point has high TPR and low FPR, so it lies near the top-left corner.

content.text: How the threshold changes predictions
This example has ten observations — five actually positive, five actually negative — each given a positive-class score. At a threshold of 0.60, any score at or above 0.60 is predicted positive.

content.caption: Figure 2. Scores above the 0.60 threshold are predicted positive; scores below it are predicted negative. Positives (circles) and negatives (squares) overlap around the cut-off.

rows: TPR usually rises, but FPR may also rise
FPR usually falls, but TPR may also fall

content.text: ROC analysis does not choose one threshold automatically — it shows the sensitivity-versus-false-alarm trade-off across all possible thresholds.
content.title: Key trade-off

content.text: Confusion matrices at two thresholds
The same model produces very different matrices depending on where the threshold sits:

content.caption: Figure 3a. A higher threshold (0.80) is stricter — fewer positives predicted, so more misses (FN) but fewer false alarms.
Figure 3b. A lower threshold (0.40) detects more positives (higher recall) but creates more false alarms (lower precision).

content.text: Worked ROC example

To construct the ROC curve, start above the maximum score (no case predicted positive), then lower the threshold one score at a time. Each newly included positive moves the curve upward; each newly included negative moves it to the right.

content.caption: Figure 4. The ROC points produced by lowering the threshold, forming a step curve well above the random-classifier diagonal (AUC = 0.68).

content.text: At threshold 0.65, this model has TPR = 0.60 and FPR = 0.40 — it detects 60% of actual positives while falsely flagging 40% of actual negatives.
content.title: Reading one point

content.text: What AUC means
AUC is a threshold-independent summary of the ROC curve, usually between 0 and 1. AUC = 1.00 is perfect ranking; AUC = 0.50 is random ranking.
AUC is the probability that a randomly selected positive example receives a higher model score than a randomly selected negative example.
content.title: Probability interpretation

content.caption: Figure 5. An illustrative AUC interpretation scale — from worse-than-random, through random (0.50), to excellent. Interpretation depends on the domain, costs, and data quality.

rows: Still check calibration, bias, external validation.
May be useful, depending on error costs.
May still look accurate on imbalanced data.
Scores or class labels may be inverted.

content.text: Calculating AUC
AUC can be computed geometrically with the trapezoidal rule after sorting ROC points by FPR, or through pairwise ranking comparisons between positive and negative cases.

content.expression: Trapezoidal: AUC = sum of trapezoid areas under the ROC curve   |   Ranking: AUC = P(score of positive > score of negative)

content.text: For the ten-observation example there are 5 × 5 = 25 positive-negative pairs. The positive score is higher in 17 of them, so AUC = 17 / 25 = 0.68.
AUC = 0.68 means the model has a 68% chance of ranking a randomly chosen positive case above a randomly chosen negative case.
content.title: Example result

content.text: Comparing classifiers with ROC curves

content.caption: Figure 6. Curves closer to the top-left corner indicate stronger discrimination — Model A (excellent) dominates Model B (good), which dominates Model C (weak).

rows: Equal or higher TPR for the same FPR across the range.
One model is better at low FPR, another at high FPR.
AUC differences may be small; test with uncertainty estimates.
High AUC but poor chosen threshold
The model ranks well, but the operating point is unsuitable.

content.text: Choosing an operating threshold
AUC compares ranking, but a deployed classifier still needs a single threshold. The best one depends on the real cost of false positives and false negatives.

items: Youden's J statistic: J = TPR − FPR; the largest J balances sensitivity and specificity when both matter equally.
Cost-based selection: choose the threshold that minimises expected financial, clinical, or operational cost.
Constraint-based selection: choose the highest TPR while keeping FPR below an allowed limit.
Validate the threshold on validation data — do not tune it on the final test set.

rows: High TPR, even with some FPR
Missing a true case may be costly.
Too many false alerts overload investigators.
Legitimate email should rarely be blocked.
Failing to detect danger can be severe.

content.text: Advantages

items: Evaluates all thresholds rather than only one cut-off.
Uses score ranking, so models with different score scales can be compared.
Separates positive-class detection (TPR) from negative-class false alarms (FPR).
AUC provides one convenient summary number for model comparison.
Useful when the relative cost of errors has not yet been fixed.

content.text: Limitations and common mistakes

rows: ROC can look optimistic because FPR divides by many negatives.
Also inspect the PR curve, precision, recall, and absolute FP counts.
Same-AUC models may differ in the important FPR range.
Compare partial ROC regions and selected operating points.
A model can rank well but output inaccurate probabilities.
Check calibration plots, Brier score, or log loss.
Use domain costs or operational constraints.
Choosing a threshold after seeing test results is optimistic.
Tune on validation; report once on untouched test data.
ROC needs continuous scores; a 0/1 prediction gives one point.

content.text: ROC-AUC measures discrimination (ranking ability) — not probability accuracy, fairness, business value, or safety by itself.
content.title: Important

content.text: ROC-AUC vs related metrics

rows: How well are positives ranked above negatives across thresholds?
What fraction of hard predictions is correct at one threshold?
Of predicted positives, how many are truly positive?
Of actual positives, how many are detected?
How well are precision and recall traded across thresholds?
Rare positive class or severe imbalance.
How accurate and confident are probabilities?

content.text: Practical workflow

items: Split data into training, validation, and test sets.
Train the classifier on the training set.
Obtain continuous probability or decision scores on validation data.
Calculate FPR and TPR at many thresholds.
Plot the ROC curve and calculate AUC.
Compare models, including confidence intervals or cross-validation variation.
Choose a threshold using costs or constraints on validation data.
Report final ROC-AUC and threshold-specific metrics on untouched test data.

content.text: Python example

content.code:
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# y_true contains 0/1 labels
# y_score contains predicted probability for class 1
fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_true, y_score)
auc_value = roc_auc_score(y_true, y_score)

plt.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"ROC-AUC = {auc_value:.3f}")
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--")
plt.xlabel("False Positive Rate")
plt.ylabel("True Positive Rate")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
content.explanation: roc_curve returns the FPR/TPR points at every threshold; roc_auc_score summarises them into a single AUC. Always pass scores, not hard 0/1 labels.

content.text: Mini interpretation example

The Random Forest has the strongest overall AUC and the lowest FPR at the shown operating point. However, the SVM may be preferred when detecting as many positives as possible matters more than controlling false alarms (it reaches TPR 0.84).
Quick revision

items: ROC plots TPR against FPR; every point corresponds to a threshold.
Top-left is desirable: high TPR and low FPR.
AUC summarises ranking across thresholds (0.50 = random, 1.00 = perfect).
AUC does not select a deployment threshold.
For severe imbalance, inspect PR-AUC and absolute false-positive counts.
Use probability or decision scores, not only hard 0/1 predictions.

content.text: The ROC curve visualises the sensitivity-versus-false-positive trade-off across thresholds, while AUC summarises how well the model ranks positive cases above negative cases.
content.title: One-sentence summary

content.text: Self-check

1. What happens to TPR and FPR when the threshold is lowered? 2. Why is the top-left corner of the ROC graph desirable? 3. What does an AUC of 0.78 mean in ranking terms? 4. Can a model have high ROC-AUC but poorly calibrated probabilities? 5. Why can PR-AUC be more informative for rare positive classes? 6. Which dataset should be used to select the final operating threshold?

keyPoints: The ROC curve plots TPR against FPR at every threshold; the top-left corner (high TPR, low FPR) is best.
AUC is a threshold-independent summary equal to the probability a random positive scores higher than a random negative (0.50 = random, 1.00 = perfect).
Lowering the threshold raises recall (TPR) but usually raises false alarms (FPR); ROC shows this trade-off without picking a threshold.
AUC compares ranking, but a deployed model still needs a threshold chosen by Youden's J, cost, or constraints — on validation data, not the test set.
On imbalanced data ROC-AUC can look optimistic, so also inspect PR-AUC; AUC measures discrimination, not calibration, cost, or fairness.
