lessons.title: Precision-Recall Curve
lessons.summary: How the precision-recall curve traces the threshold trade-off between trustworthy positive predictions (precision) and coverage of actual positives (recall), and why it is often more informative than ROC for rare positive classes. Covers the formulas and confusion-matrix effects, curve construction, a 1,000-observation worked threshold sweep, how to read and compare curves, Average Precision and AUPRC with the prevalence baseline, imbalanced-data reasoning, a PR-vs-ROC comparison and selection guide, threshold policies and applications, common mistakes, and a checklist.

content.text: Trustworthy positives vs complete coverage

When the class you care about is rare — fraud, disease, defects — the precision-recall curve is often the most honest picture of a classifier. It plots how reliable the positive predictions are (precision) against how many real positives are caught (recall), tracing that trade-off across every possible threshold instead of committing to one.
Precision focuses on false positives; recall focuses on false negatives. A PR curve summarises many thresholds and shows the trade-off between catching more positives and avoiding false alarms.
content.title: Concept preview

content.text: These notes focus specifically on the precision-recall curve for binary classification: construction, interpretation, threshold trade-offs, Average Precision, AUPRC, imbalanced-data use, and comparison with ROC curves.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define precision, recall, and the precision-recall (PR) curve.
Explain how changing a threshold produces different points on the curve.
Interpret a PR curve and identify a stronger or weaker classifier.
Understand the baseline for an imbalanced dataset.
Distinguish Average Precision (AP) from the area under a PR curve (AUPRC).
Choose an operating threshold based on the cost of false positives and false negatives.
Know when a PR curve is more informative than a ROC curve.

content.text: Core definition and formulas
A graph that plots precision on the vertical axis against recall on the horizontal axis at different classification thresholds.

content.caption: Figure 1. Precision is the reliability of predicted positives (TP among predicted positives); recall is the coverage of actual positives (TP among all real positives).

content.expression: Precision = TP / (TP + FP)   |   Recall = TP / (TP + FN)   |   F1 = 2×(P×R)/(P+R)
content.explanation: Precision answers “of predicted positives, how many are truly positive?”; recall answers “of actual positives, how many were detected?”; F1 is their harmonic balance.

rows: Not used directly in either formula

content.text: Precision is affected by false positives; recall by false negatives. True negatives appear in neither formula — one reason PR curves are useful when the negative class is very large.
content.title: Important distinction

content.text: How a PR curve is created
Most binary classifiers first produce a probability or score (such as 0.82). A decision threshold converts that score into a class prediction.

items: Obtain a score or probability for every observation.
Choose a threshold, for example 0.50.
Predict positive when score ≥ threshold; otherwise negative.
Calculate TP, FP, FN, precision, and recall.
Repeat for many thresholds from high to low.
Plot recall on the x-axis and precision on the y-axis.

content.text: What happens when the threshold changes

content.caption: Figure 2. As the threshold moves, precision rises while recall falls (and vice versa); F1 peaks in between (best F1 ≈ 0.63 here).

content.text: Lowering the threshold usually increases recall (more actual positives captured) but can reduce precision (more negatives labelled positive too).
content.title: Direction of movement

content.text: Worked threshold example
A dataset of 1,000 observations has 100 actual positives and 900 negatives — a 10% positive prevalence. The trained model gives each observation one probability score. Sweeping the threshold gives:

content.caption: Figure 3. The confusion matrix at threshold 0.50: TP = 81, FP = 43, FN = 19, TN = 857.

items: Low threshold: recall rises, but extra false positives may lower precision.
High threshold: false alarms fall, but more real positives may be missed.
The best threshold depends on application-specific error costs.

content.text: Reading and comparing PR curves

content.caption: Figure 4. An example PR curve (Average Precision = 0.864) sitting far above the random baseline of 10% (the positive-class prevalence).

items: Each point represents one classification threshold.
A point farther toward the upper-right indicates both high precision and high recall.
A curve that stays higher across most recall levels is generally better.
The left side often corresponds to strict thresholds with few predicted positives.
The right side corresponds to permissive thresholds that try to capture nearly all positives.
The curve may look step-shaped because predictions change only when the threshold passes an observed score.

content.caption: Figure 5. Stronger curves maintain higher precision for the same recall — the strong model stays near the top, the weak model hugs the 10% baseline.

content.text: The theoretical ideal is precision = 1 and recall = 1. In practice, raising recall usually means accepting more false positives, so judge the whole curve and the chosen operating point.
content.title: Ideal point

content.text: Average Precision and AUPRC
A single number is useful for comparing models, tuning hyperparameters, or reporting cross-validation. Two common summaries are Average Precision and the area under the PR curve.
A weighted average of precision values, where the increase in recall between adjacent operating points provides the weight.

content.explanation: Each precision value Pₙ is weighted by how much recall it added over the previous point.

content.text: The area under the precision-recall curve. Depending on the software it may use interpolation or the AP convention, so the reporting method should be named.

rows: Weighted average of precision over recall increments
Common in scikit-learn and information retrieval
Geometric area under the PR curve
May use trapezoidal or other interpolation
A random model's expected precision ≈ the positive rate

content.text: If only 2% of examples are positive, a random classifier's expected precision is near 0.02. So an AP of 0.25 may be a big improvement even though 0.25 looks low — always compare AP/AUPRC with the positive-class prevalence.
content.title: Baseline example

items: Compare AP/AUPRC only on the same dataset or datasets with similar class prevalence.
Use stratified cross-validation when the positive class is rare.
Report the mean and variation across folds, not only one split.
Also inspect the operating point that will actually be deployed.

content.text: Why PR curves matter for imbalanced data
A dataset is imbalanced when one class is much more common — fraud detection, disease screening, equipment failure, spam filtering, safety-event detection. There, accuracy can badly mislead.
Among 10,000 transactions with only 100 fraud cases, a model that predicts “legitimate” for everything scores 99% accuracy but 0% fraud recall — useless for the minority class.
content.title: Accuracy trap

content.text: Why the PR curve is focused

items: It concentrates on the positive class — often the class of practical interest.
It exposes false positives through precision and missed positives through recall.
It is sensitive to changes in positive-class prevalence.
It avoids being visually dominated by a very large number of true negatives.

content.text: Effect of prevalence

Because PR metrics depend on prevalence, AP values from datasets with different class balances should not be compared casually — the same model can show different precision at 1% vs 20% positives even with identical ranking ability.
content.title: Important caution

content.text: PR curve vs ROC curve
Both curves evaluate a classifier over many thresholds, but they answer different questions and use different vertical axes.

rows: Many TNs can make FPR look small
Do not report only one metric

content.text: Selection guide

items: Prefer a PR curve when the positive class is rare and positive predictions must be trustworthy.
Use ROC-AUC when ranking quality across both classes matters and balance is not extremely skewed.
For a complete evaluation, report PR-based metrics, ROC-AUC, a confusion matrix, and threshold-specific results.

content.text: Applications and threshold choice
Choosing a deployment threshold

items: Define which class is positive and why it matters.
Estimate the cost of false positives and false negatives.
Set a minimum acceptable precision or recall.
Use the PR curve to find thresholds meeting that requirement.
Check the confusion matrix and predicted-positive volume at candidate thresholds.
Validate on unseen data and monitor the metric after deployment.

content.text: Common threshold policies

rows: Alert only top 200 cases per day

content.text: Common mistakes and best practices

rows: Using the test set to choose the threshold
Choose on validation; evaluate once on test
Report positive rate and class counts
Compare on the same test set/benchmark
Rare positives can still cause many false alerts
Inspect the PR curve and precision at required recall
Evaluate calibration when probability meaning matters
F1 assumes a particular error balance
Use domain costs or explicit constraints
The curve may describe the unimportant class

content.text: A model with the highest overall AP is not always best for a specific operating region — another model may give higher precision at recall ≥ 0.95. Compare curves in the region that matches the real requirement.
content.title: Model-selection warning

content.text: Best-practice checklist

items: Use a stratified train/validation/test split for rare positive classes.
Generate the curve from continuous scores, not hard class labels.
State which class is positive.
Report prevalence, AP/AUPRC, and at least one threshold-specific confusion matrix.
Use confidence intervals or cross-validation variability for robust comparison.
Reassess thresholds when class prevalence or operational costs change.

content.text: Quick revision

rows: TP / (TP + FP): reliability of positive predictions
TP / (TP + FN): coverage of actual positives
Precision plotted against recall over many thresholds
Higher precision at the same recall; closer to upper-right
Usually increases recall and can reduce precision
Positive class, prevalence, AP/AUPRC method, curve, operating point

content.text: The precision-recall curve shows the threshold trade-off between trustworthy positive predictions and coverage of actual positives — especially useful for rare positive classes, and best interpreted with prevalence and error costs.
content.title: Final takeaway

content.text: Mini-check

1. Why can accuracy be misleading when positives are rare? 2. Which error lowers precision: FP or FN? 3. Which error lowers recall: FP or FN? 4. What happens to recall when the threshold is lowered? 5. What is the random PR baseline for a dataset with 5% positives? 6. Why should AP values from datasets with different prevalence be compared carefully? 7. When might you choose a threshold that does not maximise F1?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: A majority-class model can score high accuracy while detecting no positive cases.
False positives lower precision.
False negatives lower recall.
Recall usually increases because more cases are predicted positive.
0.05 — equal to the positive-class prevalence.
Precision, and therefore AP, depends on class prevalence.
When domain costs, legal requirements, safety targets, or operational capacity require a different precision-recall balance.

keyPoints: The PR curve plots precision against recall over many thresholds; better models stay higher (closer to the upper-right) for the same recall.
Precision is hurt by false positives and recall by false negatives; true negatives appear in neither, so PR is ideal when the negative class is huge.
The PR baseline is the positive-class prevalence, so AP/AUPRC must be read relative to prevalence and compared only across similar distributions.
Lowering the threshold usually raises recall and can lower precision; choose the operating point by error costs or constraints, not by default 0.50.
For rare positives the PR curve is more informative than ROC, which can look optimistic because of the many true negatives.
commonMistakes: Reporting AP/AUPRC without stating the positive-class prevalence, hiding the baseline.
Comparing AP across datasets with different class balance.
Building the curve from hard 0/1 labels instead of continuous scores.
Choosing the deployment threshold on the test set instead of validation data.

lessons.title: Learning Curves
lessons.summary: How learning curves diagnose a model by plotting training and validation performance against training-set size. Covers construction, why the two curves diverge and converge, the generalization gap (score- and loss-based), the underfitting / overfitting / good-fit patterns with a decision flow, an email-spam worked example, when more data will help, cross-validation practice and a scikit-learn learning_curve example, metric choice, common mistakes, and the learning-curve-vs-validation-curve distinction.

content.text: Diagnosing a model with data

A learning curve is a simple but powerful diagnostic: train the model on more and more data, and watch how its training and validation scores move. Where they end up — and the gap between them — tells you whether the model is held back by too little data, too little capacity, or too much complexity, so you can pick the right fix instead of guessing.

content.caption: Figure 1. A learning curve plots training and validation performance against training-set size — the training score falls slightly while the validation score rises, and they converge.

content.text: The curve answers a practical question: is the model limited by too little data, too little model capacity, or excessive model complexity?
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on learning curves as a model-evaluation and validation tool.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define a learning curve and identify its axes, lines, and performance measures.
Explain how training and validation scores change as training data grows.
Diagnose underfitting (high bias), overfitting (high variance), and good fit.
Decide whether more data, different complexity, better features, or regularization will help.
Generate and interpret a learning curve using cross-validation.

content.text: Definition
A graph showing how a model's performance changes as the number of training examples increases — normally plotting both the training score and the validation score against training-set size.

rows: Amount of data used to train
Number or percentage of training examples
Accuracy, F1, R², negative error, log-loss

content.text: How learning curves are constructed

content.caption: Figure 2. The basic process: create increasing training subsets → train on each → measure training and validation scores → plot against size → diagnose bias, variance, and data need.

items: Split data into training and validation portions, or use cross-validation.
Select increasing training sizes (e.g. 10%, 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 100%).
Train the same model at each selected size.
Measure performance on the training subset and on unseen validation data.
Average the scores across cross-validation folds when possible.
Plot the mean training and validation scores against the number of training examples.

content.text: Keep the model, preprocessing, evaluation metric, and cross-validation method consistent across all training sizes — otherwise the curves are not comparable.
content.title: Important control

content.text: Why the two curves behave differently

rows: Model memorises a small sample but hasn't seen enough variation
Model nears its achievable performance for current features/complexity

content.caption: Figure 3. A healthy learning curve: training and validation scores converge at a high value as data grows.

content.text: Scores and the generalization gap
At training size m, S_train(m) is the average score on the training subset and S_val(m) is the average on unseen validation data. The generalization gap is their difference (when higher is better):

content.explanation: For error or loss metrics (lower is better) the direction reverses: validation loss is usually higher than training loss.

content.caption: Figure 4. Learning curves based on loss rather than accuracy — training loss rises slightly and validation loss falls as data grows, both converging (lower is better).

content.text: Interpreting common patterns
Underfitting (high bias)

content.caption: Figure 5. Underfitting: training and validation scores are close but both low — the model can't fit even the training data well.

items: The training score is low, so the model can't fit even the training data well.
The validation score is also low and usually close to the training score.
Adding much more data alone is unlikely to solve the main problem.

content.text: Overfitting (high variance)

content.caption: Figure 6. Overfitting: training performance stays much higher than validation, and the large gap persists even as more data is added.

items: The training score is high while the validation score is considerably lower.
The gap remains large even as more training examples are added.
The model has learned details or noise that do not generalise well.

content.text: Good fit

items: Training and validation scores are both high.
The gap is small enough for the application.
Both curves have reached a plateau, so adding data may give only limited gains.
Further improvement may need better features, a different model family, or better labels.

content.text: A small gap is desirable only when both scores are high. A small gap with two low scores usually indicates underfitting, not a good model.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Quick diagnostic decision flow

content.caption: Figure 7. A practical decision flow: both scores low and close → underfitting; large gap → overfitting; high and close → good fit.

content.text: If underfitting — likely causes and responses

rows: Use a more flexible algorithm or increase capacity.
Create better features or include relevant variables.
Train longer or improve optimisation when relevant.

content.text: If overfitting — useful responses

rows: Reduces dependence on accidental patterns in a small set.
Adds realistic variation for image, audio, and text tasks.
Gives a more reliable estimate and detects leakage.

content.text: Worked example: email spam classifier
A logistic-regression model classifies emails as spam or not spam, with accuracy measured by five-fold cross-validation. As the training set grows:

content.caption: Figure 8. The spam classifier's learning curve — validation accuracy climbs from 0.60 to 0.84 while the gap shrinks toward zero.

content.text: The model initially overfits (training score much higher than validation). As data is added, validation accuracy rises and the gap shrinks. By 1,200 examples it generalises well, and further data may give only small gains.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Will more data help?

rows: More data may reduce variance and improve generalisation.
The model is biased — capacity or features are the bigger problem.
The model is near its current performance ceiling.
More representative data can stabilise estimates; verify split quality.
Possible distribution shift, leakage, or label-quality problems.

content.text: “More data” means more relevant, correctly labelled, and representative data. Large amounts of biased or low-quality data may not improve the model.
content.title: Key caution

content.text: Learning curves with cross-validation
Cross-validation produces a more reliable learning curve than a single holdout because each training size is evaluated across several folds.

items: Classification: use stratified folds when class proportions should be preserved.
Time series: do not shuffle future observations into training — use time-aware splits.
Grouped data: keep related observations (e.g. same patient) in the same fold.
Preprocessing: fit scalers, encoders, and feature selection inside each training fold via a pipeline.
Report variability: show standard deviation or confidence bands for detailed analysis.

content.text: Python example (scikit-learn)

content.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

train_sizes, train_scores, val_scores = learning_curve(
    estimator=model, X=X, y=y,
    train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 8),
    cv=cv, scoring='accuracy', n_jobs=-1
)

train_mean = train_scores.mean(axis=1)
val_mean = val_scores.mean(axis=1)

plt.plot(train_sizes, train_mean, marker='o', label='Training score')
plt.plot(train_sizes, val_mean, marker='o', label='Validation score')
plt.xlabel('Training examples'); plt.ylabel('Accuracy'); plt.legend(); plt.show()
content.explanation: learning_curve trains the model at each size across the CV folds; train_sizes sets the fractions, and the pipeline keeps preprocessing leakage-safe inside each fold.

content.text: Choosing the right metric

rows: Fine when classes and error costs are balanced.
Accuracy can hide poor minority performance.
For error metrics, lower actual error is better.
Evaluates confidence, not just the final label.
Match the metric to class balance and goal.

content.text: Common mistakes

rows: The shape may depend heavily on that split.
Points no longer measure one consistent model.
Keep the configuration fixed for diagnosis.
Information can leak from validation data.
A high curve may still ignore the minority class.
Inspect both absolute level and gap.
Use several ordered sizes from small to full.
A mean curve can hide instability.
Add uncertainty bands or report fold variation.
Future information leaks into past training.

content.text: Learning curve vs validation curve

rows: Score vs tree depth or regularization

content.text: A learning curve changes the amount of training data. A validation curve changes a model hyperparameter while usually keeping the dataset fixed. Do not confuse them.
content.title: Do not confuse them

content.text: Interpretation checklist

items: What metric is on the y-axis, and is higher or lower better?
Are the scores averaged across suitable cross-validation folds?
Are both training and validation scores high, moderate, or low?
Is the gap large, small, shrinking, or increasing?
Are the curves still changing at the largest training size?
Would more representative data likely improve validation performance?
Could leakage, class imbalance, grouping, or time order be distorting the curve?
What is the best next action: more data, better features, a simpler model, or a more flexible model?

content.text: Key highlights

items: Learning curves compare training and validation performance across increasing training-set sizes.
Low and close curves usually indicate underfitting; high training with a large gap usually indicates overfitting.
More data is most promising when the validation score is improving and the gap is shrinking.
The absolute score level, the gap, the slope, and the plateau must be interpreted together.

content.text: Quick revision

rows: The number or proportion of training examples.
A model-performance score or error measure.
What does a large gap suggest?
What do low, close scores suggest?
When is more data likely to help?
When validation is rising and the gap is shrinking.
When may more data help little?
When both curves are low and close, or already flat and high.
To get a more stable estimate across multiple splits.
Learning varies data size; validation varies a hyperparameter.

content.text: Read four features together: the level of both curves, the gap between them, the direction of change, and whether they have reached a plateau.
content.title: Final takeaway

content.text: Mini self-test

1. Training accuracy 98%, validation 70%, gap stays large — likely issue? 2. Training and validation both stabilise near 62% — likely issue? 3. Validation accuracy still rising at the largest size while the gap shrinks — what to consider? 4. Why place preprocessing inside a cross-validation pipeline? 5. Which curve changes model complexity instead of data size?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: Overfitting / high variance.
Underfitting / high bias.
Collecting more representative training data.
To prevent information leakage from validation folds.
A validation curve.

keyPoints: A learning curve plots training and validation scores against training-set size to reveal whether a model is data-limited, under-capacity, or over-complex.
Low, close curves signal underfitting (high bias); a high training score with a large persistent gap signals overfitting (high variance).
A small gap only means a good fit when both scores are high; interpret level, gap, slope, and plateau together.
More data mainly helps when the validation score is still rising and the gap is shrinking — and only if that data is relevant and well-labelled.
Build the curve with cross-validation and preprocessing inside a pipeline; a learning curve varies data size, while a validation curve varies a hyperparameter.

Changing hyperparameters at each training size, so points no longer measure one model.

Covers construction and the mean-score calculation, reading the three regions, a decision-tree max_depth worked example, the generalization gap, commonly studied hyperparameters and the direction-of-complexity caution, validation-curve-vs-learning-curve and vs-grid-search comparisons, a scikit-learn validation_curve example, how to choose the best value (plateau principle), best practices, common mistakes, special cases, and an SVM-C mini case study.

content.text: Tuning one dial at a time

A validation curve isolates a single hyperparameter — tree depth, regularization strength, number of neighbours — and shows exactly how training and validation performance respond as you turn that one dial. It's the clearest way to see whether a model is too simple, too complex, or just right, and to pick a defensible setting instead of guessing.
A validation curve plots model performance on the training data and cross-validation data while one hyperparameter is varied across a range of values.
content.title: One-line definition

content.text: These notes stay focused on validation curves: what they show, how to construct them, how to read underfitting and overfitting, and how to use them for hyperparameter selection.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define a validation curve in simple terms.
Explain the roles of training score, validation score, and model complexity.
Identify underfitting, a suitable complexity region, and overfitting from a graph.
Use a validation curve to select a reasonable hyperparameter value.
Distinguish validation curves from learning curves and grid search.
Implement a validation curve with scikit-learn.

content.text: What is a validation curve?
For each chosen hyperparameter value, the model is trained and evaluated (normally with cross-validation), and two average scores are plotted:

items: Training score: performance on the data used to fit the model.
Validation score: performance on held-out folds that simulate unseen data.

content.text: The horizontal axis holds values of one hyperparameter (tree depth, regularization strength, number of neighbours, polynomial degree); the vertical axis holds a metric such as accuracy, F1, R², or negative RMSE.

rows: A model setting chosen before training (e.g. max_depth, C).
The model's flexibility to fit detailed patterns.
Average score on each training fold.
Average score on each held-out validation fold.
Difference between training and validation performance.
A stable area with strong validation performance and an acceptable gap.

content.text: The highest training score is not the goal. A useful model should perform strongly on unseen data — the validation score.
content.title: Important

content.text: Why validation curves are useful

items: Reveal whether a model is too simple or too complex.
Show the direction in which a hyperparameter should be adjusted.
Help narrow the search range before a larger tuning procedure.
Expose a high-variance model through a large training-validation gap.
Provide a visual explanation of the bias-variance trade-off.
Support a defensible hyperparameter choice rather than guessing.

content.text: How a validation curve is created

content.caption: Figure 1. The workflow: choose one hyperparameter → select a value range → train with cross-validation → record train & validation scores → plot and select the best region. Only one hyperparameter varies; other settings stay fixed.

items: Choose a model and one hyperparameter to investigate.
Create a sensible sequence of hyperparameter values.
For each value, run k-fold cross-validation.
Calculate the mean training score and mean validation score.
Optionally calculate the standard deviation across folds.
Plot both mean scores against the hyperparameter values.
Select a stable value or region with strong validation performance.

content.expression: Mean validation score = (score₁ + score₂ + score₃ + score₄ + score₅) ÷ 5
content.explanation: For 5-fold CV, each hyperparameter value gives five training and five validation scores; the plotted point is the mean. Error bands of mean ± one standard deviation show stability — wide bands mean the result changes a lot across folds.

content.text: Reading a validation curve

content.caption: Figure 2. An example validation curve for decision-tree max_depth: an underfitting region (low, close scores), a good range (validation peaks at depth 5), and an overfitting region (training near-perfect, validation falling).

content.text: Underfitting region (high bias)

items: Training and validation scores are both relatively low.
The two curves are often close together.
The model is not flexible enough to learn the main pattern.
Action: increase complexity or reduce excessive regularization.

content.text: Suitable complexity region

items: Validation score reaches a high level or a stable plateau.
Training score is also good, but not necessarily perfect.
The generalization gap remains manageable.
Prefer a simpler value within a performance plateau when scores are very similar.

content.text: Overfitting region (high variance)

items: Training score becomes very high, sometimes nearly perfect.
Validation score stops improving and may decrease.
The gap between the curves becomes large.
Action: decrease complexity, strengthen regularization, or collect more useful data.

content.caption: Figure 3. Simplified patterns: underfitting (both scores low and close), good fit (validation high, gap small), and overfitting (training high, validation dropping).

content.text: Worked example: decision-tree depth
A decision-tree classifier predicts whether a customer will accept an offer. We choose max_depth, measuring accuracy with 5-fold stratified cross-validation.

items: Depths 1–2: both scores are low, so the tree is too shallow.
Depths 3–5: validation accuracy improves strongly and the gap stays moderate.
Depth 5: validation accuracy reaches its maximum of 0.90.
Depths 6–10: training accuracy keeps rising, but validation accuracy falls.
Conclusion: deeper trees memorise training details and generalise poorly.

content.text: max_depth = 5 gives the highest validation accuracy here, but max_depth = 4 may be chosen when simplicity, stability, and interpretability matter, since its score (0.88) is close to the maximum.
content.title: Selection

content.text: The generalization gap

content.expression: Generalization gap = Training score − Validation score

rows: Keep the setting; verify on a test set.
Use repeated CV; inspect data and folds.

content.text: A small gap is not automatically good — if both scores are poor, the model is simply underfitting.
content.title: Caution

content.text: Hyperparameters commonly studied

rows: Large k underfits; small k overfits
Large C overfits; small C underfits

content.text: The x-axis does not always run from simple to complex in the same direction. Larger max_depth or C usually means MORE complexity; larger k-NN n_neighbors or regularization alpha usually means a SIMPLER model. Always determine the direction before interpreting the curves.
content.title: Direction matters

content.text: Validation curve vs learning curve

content.caption: Figure 4. A validation curve varies one hyperparameter (fixed data size); a learning curve varies the training-set size (fixed hyperparameters).

rows: Would more data or a different model help?

content.text: Validation curve vs grid search

rows: Understand one parameter, choose a range
Lower when many combinations are tested

content.text: Use a validation curve to understand an important hyperparameter, then use grid or randomized search for final multi-parameter tuning inside a sensible range.
content.title: Good workflow

content.text: Python example (scikit-learn)
This studies max_depth for a decision-tree classifier. A pipeline keeps preprocessing inside each fold to prevent leakage.

content.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, validation_curve
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42))
values = np.arange(1, 11)
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

train_scores, valid_scores = validation_curve(
    model, X, y,
    param_name="decisiontreeclassifier__max_depth",
    param_range=values, cv=cv, scoring="accuracy", n_jobs=-1
)

train_mean, valid_mean = train_scores.mean(axis=1), valid_scores.mean(axis=1)
plt.plot(values, train_mean, marker="o", label="Training")
plt.plot(values, valid_mean, marker="o", label="Validation")
plt.xlabel("max_depth"); plt.ylabel("Accuracy"); plt.legend(); plt.show()
content.explanation: train_scores / valid_scores are matrices (one row per value, one column per fold); mean(axis=1) gives the plotted line and std(axis=1) the uncertainty band.

content.text: For imbalanced classification, accuracy may hide poor minority performance — consider scoring="f1", "roc_auc", or "average_precision". For regression, use "r2", "neg_mean_absolute_error", or "neg_root_mean_squared_error" (scikit-learn negates loss metrics so larger is still better).
content.title: Metric note

content.text: Choosing the best value
Do not mechanically pick the single highest point. Use this practical sequence:

items: Find the region with the highest or near-highest validation score.
Check whether the training-validation gap is acceptable.
Inspect the error bands or fold-to-fold variation.
Prefer a simpler value when several settings perform similarly.
Confirm the selected setting with nested CV or a separate final test set when needed.
Evaluate secondary requirements: speed, memory, interpretability, fairness, calibration.

content.text: When validation performance forms a plateau, choose a simpler point near the start of that plateau rather than the most complex point.
content.title: Plateau principle

content.text: Best practices

rows: A single split may produce a misleading curve.
Preserves class proportions in each fold.
Use time-aware splits for time series
Random folds can leak future information.
The curve should reflect the real objective.
C, gamma, alpha span orders of magnitude.
The test set is for final unbiased evaluation.
Reduces dependence on one fold arrangement.

content.text: Common mistakes

items: Using the test set to build the curve — leaks test information into model selection.
Changing several hyperparameters at once — the effect of one setting becomes unclear.
Choosing only by training score — strongly favours overfitting.
Using a poor parameter range — the optimum may lie outside the plotted values.
Ignoring parameter scale — linear spacing may be unsuitable for C, alpha, or gamma.
Ignoring error bars — a tiny difference in mean score may not be meaningful.
Preprocessing before cross-validation — global scaling or selection can leak information.
Assuming the curve proves causality — it only describes performance under the chosen data, metric, model, and CV design.
Using random CV for temporal data — future observations may influence the past.
Selecting a complex point from a flat plateau — adds complexity without reliable benefit.

content.text: Special considerations

rows: Use stratified folds and suitable metrics — accuracy can look strong while the minority class is predicted poorly.
Use TimeSeriesSplit or chronological validation; train only on observations available before each validation period.
Scores fluctuate — use repeated CV, confidence intervals, and conservative parameter choices.
p values × k folds ≈ p×k models; use a smaller range, parallelism, or a preliminary sample.
One metric may not capture all needs (e.g. fraud may need recall AND precision curves, plus latency and calibration).

content.text: Mini case study: SVM regularization
An SVM classifier is tested with C = [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100]. Larger C means weaker regularization and usually a more flexible boundary.
C = 1 is the strongest candidate. C = 0.1 may be preferred for a simpler, more regularized model with only a small performance reduction.
content.title: Interpretation

content.text: Interpretation checklist

rows: One hyperparameter and its relationship to complexity.
A metric where the direction of “better” is clear.
Is the best point on an edge?
If not, leakage may invalidate the curve.

content.text: Quick revision

items: Low, close scores usually indicate high bias.
A high validation score with a moderate gap indicates useful generalisation.
A high training score with a falling validation score indicates high variance.
The selected value should be strong, stable, and no more complex than necessary.
Cross-validation, correct metrics, leakage-safe pipelines, and an untouched test set are essential.

content.text: A validation curve is a one-hyperparameter diagnostic tool: it compares training and cross-validation performance to reveal underfitting, a suitable complexity region, and overfitting.
content.title: Remember

content.text: Compact glossary

rows: Error from an overly simple model.
Repeated train-validation splitting for reliable estimation.
Range where validation performance changes very little.

content.text: Self-check

1. What does a validation curve plot? 2. What indicates underfitting? 3. What indicates overfitting? 4. Why is cross-validation preferred? 5. Why should preprocessing be inside a pipeline? 6. What should you do if the best score is at the largest tested value? 7. How is a validation curve different from a learning curve? 8. Why might the simplest near-best point be selected?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: Training and cross-validation performance against values of one hyperparameter.
Training and validation scores both low and often close.
Training performance high, validation lower or falling, and a large gap.
It reduces dependence on one arbitrary train-validation split.
To prevent information from validation folds influencing training transformations.
Extend the range, unless domain or resource constraints justify stopping.
A validation curve varies a hyperparameter; a learning curve varies training-set size.
It may give similar generalisation with lower variance, cost, and complexity.

keyPoints: A validation curve varies ONE hyperparameter (data size fixed) and plots training and cross-validation scores to reveal under/over-fitting.
Low, close scores mean high bias; a high training score with a large, growing gap means high variance; the good region has a high validation score and manageable gap.
Know each hyperparameter's direction of complexity first — larger max_depth/C means more complex, but larger k-NN n_neighbors or alpha means simpler.
Don't just pick the peak: prefer a simpler value on a plateau, check error bands, and confirm with nested CV or a held-out test set.
Build the curve with cross-validation and a leakage-safe pipeline; a validation curve tunes complexity, a learning curve diagnoses data sufficiency, and grid search does final multi-parameter tuning.
commonMistakes: Using the test set (not validation/CV) to build the curve, leaking information into model selection.
Varying several hyperparameters at once, so one setting's effect is unclear.
Choosing by training score alone, favouring overfitting.
Preprocessing before cross-validation instead of inside a pipeline.

lessons.title: Overfitting and Underfitting
lessons.summary: The two failure modes of model fitting: underfitting (too simple, high bias, poor on both training and unseen data) and overfitting (too flexible, high variance, great on training but poor on unseen data). Covers definitions and signs, a side-by-side comparison, the model-complexity bias-variance trade-off, diagnosing from training vs validation results, the generalization gap, learning-curve patterns, causes, remedies for each, model-specific controls, a three-model worked example, correct validation practice, scikit-learn validation-curve and GridSearchCV examples, misconceptions, and a checklist.

content.text: Signal, not noise

Every model sits somewhere on a spectrum. Too simple and it misses the real pattern (underfitting); too flexible and it memorises the training data's noise (overfitting). The whole craft of model evaluation is finding the middle — a model that learns the signal and still generalises to data it has never seen.

content.caption: Figure 1. The same data fit three ways: underfitting (a line too simple to follow the pattern), a good fit (captures the trend and generalises), and overfitting (a wiggly curve that chases every point).

content.text: A model should learn the underlying relationship (signal) in the training data and use it successfully on unseen data. A high training score alone does not prove that a model generalises.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on overfitting and underfitting. Bias, variance, learning curves, regularization, cross-validation, and early stopping appear only where they help diagnose or solve these two problems.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define underfitting and overfitting in clear terms.
Recognise each from training, validation, and test performance.
Explain the relationship with model complexity, bias, and variance.
Interpret learning curves and validation curves.
Select practical methods to reduce underfitting or overfitting.
Avoid data leakage and invalid model-selection practices.

content.text: Underfitting
The condition where a model cannot represent or learn the important structure in the data — it performs poorly on both the training set and unseen validation/test sets.
Typical signs

items: Poor training performance — the model hasn't even fitted its training examples.
Poor validation performance — unseen-data performance is also weak.
Small generalization gap — training and validation scores may be close, but both are unsatisfactory.
High bias — the model makes strong simplifying assumptions and misses useful patterns.
Limited improvement from more data — more examples help little unless capacity or features improve.

content.text: Example: house price depends nonlinearly on size, location, age, and condition. A model that predicts every house with the average price, or a straight line based only on size, misses important structure — its errors stay large even on the training data.
Overfitting
The condition where a model fits the training data extremely closely — including noise, outliers, or accidental details — but performs worse on unseen validation/test data.
Typical signs

items: Very strong training performance — training error is very low or the training score unusually high.
Weak validation performance — the model can't reproduce its training success on unseen data.
Large generalization gap — validation error is much higher than training error.
High variance — small changes in the training sample can produce noticeably different models.
Unstable predictions — the model reacts strongly to noise, outliers, or small feature changes.

content.text: Example: a degree-14 polynomial can pass close to every point in a small dataset, giving a near-perfect training fit — but its curve oscillates wildly between points and predicts poorly for new examples. It has memorised local details, not a stable relationship.
Underfitting vs overfitting

content.caption: Figure 2. The bias-variance view: underfitting = high bias/low variance, balanced fit = moderate both, overfitting = low bias/high variance with a large generalization gap.

content.text: Model complexity and the bias-variance trade-off
Model complexity is how flexible a model is — polynomial degree, tree depth, number of parameters, neural-network layers, or the inverse strength of regularization.

items: Low complexity → high bias: the model can't capture enough structure, so underfitting is likely.
High complexity → high variance: the model adapts to small training details, so overfitting is likely.
Suitable complexity: validation error is minimised and generalisation is strongest.

content.caption: Figure 3. Training error keeps falling as complexity rises, while validation error follows a U-shape — the minimum marks the best generalisation.

content.text: Diagnosing from training and validation results
Use the same metric for training and validation — the pattern, not just the absolute number, identifies the problem.

rows: The model can't fit the training signal.
Sampling variation, leakage, or easier validation data.

content.caption: Figure 4. A first-response flowchart: poor/poor → underfitting (add capacity); strong/strong → appropriate fit (confirm on test); strong/weak → overfitting (simplify, regularize, add data). Diagnose with unseen data, not training performance alone.

content.text: The generalization gap

content.expression: Generalization gap = validation performance − training performance
content.explanation: For an error metric, a large positive gap (validation error ≫ training error) suggests overfitting. For a score (higher is better), a large negative gap (validation score ≪ training score) suggests overfitting.

content.text: Learning curves
A learning curve plots training and validation performance against the number of training examples — showing whether the model would benefit more from additional data or from a design change.

content.caption: Figure 5. Underfitting curves converge low (more data helps little); overfitting curves keep a high training score with a persistent gap (more representative data may reduce it).

items: Underfitting pattern: training and validation converge at a low level — more data alone rarely solves the core problem.
Overfitting pattern: training high, validation lower, and a gap remains — more representative data may reduce the gap.
Healthy pattern: validation improves and approaches training at a strong level.

content.text: Common causes

rows: Model is too complex for the dataset size
Too many weak or noisy features
Training too many epochs without early stopping
Decision tree too deep or with tiny leaves
Data leakage creates falsely strong results

content.text: How to reduce underfitting

items: Use a more expressive model — higher polynomial degree, deeper tree, more capacity, or a model suited to nonlinear structure.
Improve features — add relevant variables, interactions, transformations, or domain-informed representations.
Reduce excessive regularization — lower L1/L2 strength, relax pruning, or reduce dropout when too strong.
Train more effectively — more epochs, better learning rate, improved optimisation, and check convergence.
Fix preprocessing — scale when needed, encode categories correctly, don't discard informative data.
Review the target and metric — a noisy or mis-defined target can look like underfitting.

content.text: How to reduce overfitting

items: Collect more representative data — varied examples make memorisation harder.
Use data augmentation — realistic transformed examples for images, audio, or text.
Simplify the model — fewer degrees, less depth, fewer features/layers/neurons/parameters.
Apply regularization — L1/L2 penalties, dropout, pruning, minimum leaf size, margin control.
Use early stopping — stop when validation performance stops improving.
Perform cross-validation — select hyperparameters over multiple folds, not one lucky split.
Use feature selection — remove irrelevant, duplicate, or noisy variables.
Use ensembles carefully — bagging and random forests reduce variance; unrestricted boosting can still overfit.
Prevent data leakage — fit preprocessing only on training folds; keep test data separate.

content.text: Model-specific controls

rows: Deeper trees or more useful features
Increase k; scale features; drop noisy dims
Increase C or a more suitable kernel
Reduce C; lower gamma for RBF
Dropout, weight decay, augmentation, early stopping

content.text: Worked evaluation example
Three models are trained for the same balanced binary-classification task, measured by accuracy:

Model C has the best training accuracy but the worst generalization gap. Model B has lower training accuracy yet stronger validation performance — making it the better candidate for unseen data. The best model is not the one with the lowest training error.
content.title: Why Model B wins

content.text: Correct validation practice

items: Split data into training and final test sets (or a separate validation set when data is sufficient).
Build preprocessing and the model in one pipeline so each fold is processed independently.
Use cross-validation on training data to compare complexity and hyperparameters.
Choose the final configuration based on cross-validated performance and stability.
Fit the chosen pipeline on all available training data.
Evaluate once on the untouched test set to estimate final generalisation.

content.text: Trying many models and repeatedly picking the one that looks best on the same validation set can indirectly overfit that validation set. Nested cross-validation or a final untouched test set reduces this risk.
content.title: Validation-set overfitting

content.text: Python: validation curve for complexity
Varying decision-tree depth — a shallow tree may underfit, a very deep tree may overfit, and the cross-validated score finds a suitable range.

content.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import validation_curve
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
import numpy as np

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
depths = np.arange(1, 16)

train_scores, val_scores = validation_curve(
    DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42), X, y,
    param_name="max_depth", param_range=depths,
    cv=5, scoring="accuracy"
)

best_depth = depths[np.argmax(val_scores.mean(axis=1))]
print("Best cross-validated depth:", best_depth)
content.explanation: Small depths may underfit (both scores low); as depth rises both improve until validation peaks; at large depths training keeps rising while validation falls — overfitting. Choose the depth by cross-validation, never by repeatedly inspecting the test set.

content.text: Python: pipeline and regularization

For logistic regression, smaller C means stronger regularization — very small C can underfit, very large C can overfit. GridSearchCV compares settings across folds while keeping scaling inside the pipeline.

content.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000))
])

search = GridSearchCV(
    pipe,
    param_grid={"model__C": [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100]},
    scoring="f1", cv=5
)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(search.best_params_, search.best_score_)

content.text: Common misconceptions

rows: 100% training accuracy means the model is excellent.
It may be memorisation — check validation/test and the gap.
More complex models are always better.
Complexity helps only until validation stops improving.
Underfitting usually needs better features, capacity, or optimisation.
Too much regularization can cause underfitting.
A small train-validation gap always means success.
The two may be close because both are poor.
It improves estimation, but repeated tuning can still overfit.
Test data can be used to choose hyperparameters.
The test set must stay untouched until final evaluation.

content.text: Practical checklist

items: Is training performance poor? Consider underfitting.
Is validation much worse than training? Consider overfitting.
Are preprocessing steps fitted only on training folds?
Is the validation/test split representative and stratified when needed?
Have multiple metrics been checked for imbalanced classification?
Have learning curves or validation curves been inspected?
Has model complexity been tuned through cross-validation?
Is the final test set still untouched?
Are results stable across folds or random seeds?
Does the selected model make domain sense, not only numerical sense?

content.text: Key highlights

rows: Poor training + poor validation = not enough useful structure learned.
Excellent training + much weaker validation = training-specific detail learned.
Pick the model that performs best and most consistently on unseen validation folds — not the one that memorises the training set.

content.text: Underfitting fails to learn enough signal; overfitting learns training-specific noise. Select suitable complexity with validation and cross-validation, then confirm generalisation once on an untouched test set.
content.title: Final summary

content.text: Quick self-check

1. A model has 62% training and 61% validation accuracy — most likely problem? 2. Training RMSE 0.2, validation RMSE 5.1 — what does this suggest? 3. Why can excessive L2 regularization cause underfitting? 4. Which curve often has a U-shape as complexity increases? 5. Why must the final test set remain untouched during model selection?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: Likely underfitting (if 62% is inadequate) — the scores are close but both weak.
Strong overfitting — training error is extremely low while unseen-data error is much larger.
It constrains coefficients too strongly, preventing the model from representing useful relationships.
Validation error — it may first decrease then increase as complexity becomes excessive.
To obtain an unbiased final estimate of generalisation after all model choices are complete.

keyPoints: Underfitting = high bias: poor on both training and validation; overfitting = high variance: strong on training but much weaker on validation.
As model complexity rises, training error keeps falling but validation error is U-shaped — the minimum is the best generalisation.
Diagnose from the pattern of training vs validation results, not the absolute number — a small gap only means success when both scores are high.
Cure underfitting with more capacity/features/less regularization; cure overfitting with more data, simpler models, regularization, and early stopping.
Select complexity with cross-validation and a leakage-safe pipeline, then confirm generalisation once on an untouched test set.
commonMistakes: Treating high (even 100%) training accuracy as proof of a good model, ignoring the validation gap.
Assuming more data will fix underfitting when better features or capacity are actually needed.
Using too much regularization and causing underfitting.
Repeatedly tuning on the test set (or the same validation set), overfitting the model-selection process.

lessons.title: Bias-Variance Trade-off
lessons.summary: The balance between systematic error from an overly simple model (bias) and instability from an overly flexible model (variance). Covers definitions and signs of each, the target analogy, the Bias² + Variance + Irreducible-Noise decomposition, how complexity shifts bias and variance (U-shaped test error), a polynomial-degree visual, a three-model worked example, diagnosing from scores, remedies for high bias and high variance, regularization's effect, algorithm tendencies, the role of cross-validation and learning curves, misconceptions, and a checklist.

content.text: Two ways a model can fail

Prediction error comes from two competing sources. A model that is too simple is systematically wrong no matter the data (bias); a model that is too flexible swings wildly with each new sample (variance). Lower one and the other tends to rise — the bias-variance trade-off is finding the balance where total error on unseen data is lowest.
A useful model must be flexible enough to learn the real pattern but stable enough not to memorise random noise. The bias-variance trade-off describes this balance.
content.title: Core idea

content.text: These notes stay focused on the bias-variance trade-off and its role in model evaluation.
content.title: Scope

content.text: What you'll be able to do

items: Define bias and variance in machine learning.
Explain why decreasing bias can increase variance, and vice versa.
Interpret training and validation performance patterns.
Identify underfitting, good generalisation, and overfitting.
Apply practical methods to reduce high bias or high variance.

content.text: Definition
The balance between two major sources of prediction error: systematic error from an overly simple model (bias) and instability from excessive sensitivity to the training sample (variance).

rows: Error from assumptions that are too simple or rigid.
Error from reacting too strongly to small data changes.
Adjusting flexibility so both errors are acceptably low.

content.text: Bias: systematic error
Bias measures how far the model's average prediction is from the true relationship. High bias usually means the model is too simple for the data.

items: High training error and high validation error.
Training and validation scores are often close, but both are poor.
The model fails to capture non-linear patterns, interactions, or relevant features.
Common example: fitting a straight line to a strongly curved relationship.

content.text: Variance: sensitivity to data
Variance measures how much a model's predictions would change if it were trained on a different sample from the same population. High variance means the model is unstable.

items: Very low training error but noticeably higher validation/test error.
A large gap exists between training and validation performance.
Small changes in the dataset may produce very different fitted models.
Common example: a deep decision tree that memorises training examples.

content.text: The target analogy
Picture repeated model predictions as shots at a target whose centre is the true value. Bias is how far the cluster sits from the centre; variance is how spread out the shots are.

content.caption: Figure 1. Bias describes distance from the centre; variance describes spread between predictions. The ideal is low bias and low variance (tight cluster on the bullseye).

rows: Accurate and consistent — the ideal case.
Average near the truth but unstable — overfitting risk.
Both wrong and unstable — poor model or pipeline.

content.text: Mathematical error decomposition
For squared-error regression, the expected prediction error at an input can be decomposed conceptually as:

content.expression: Expected Test Error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible Noise
content.explanation: Reduce bias with more useful flexibility or better features; reduce variance with regularization, more data, pruning, or averaging; irreducible noise cannot be fully removed.

rows: Squared systematic gap between average prediction and truth.
Yes — more useful flexibility or better features.
Change in predictions across different training samples.
Yes — regularization, more data, pruning, averaging.
Not completely; better measurements may reduce part.

content.text: The decomposition is exact under specific assumptions for squared-error regression. In classification, the same idea helps explain generalisation, but the exact decomposition is more complex.
content.title: Clarification

content.text: How complexity changes bias and variance
As model complexity increases, bias usually falls (the model can represent richer relationships) but variance usually rises (the model becomes more sensitive to the exact training sample).

items: Low complexity → high bias: cannot capture enough structure, so underfitting is likely.
High complexity → high variance: adapts to small training details, so overfitting is likely.
Suitable complexity: validation error is minimised and generalisation is strongest.

content.caption: Figure 2. Bias² falls and variance rises with complexity; expected test error is U-shaped, and its minimum — the best trade-off — sits at an intermediate complexity.

content.text: The goal is not to minimise training error — it is to minimise error on unseen data.
content.title: Key highlight

content.text: Visual example: polynomial regression
The same dataset produces very different models depending on polynomial degree, which controls flexibility.

content.caption: Figure 3. Degree 1 is too simple and misses the pattern; degree 12 is too complex and follows noise; degree 3 captures the underlying trend.

content.text: Worked example
Three regression models predict house prices (lower RMSE is better):

Linear regression has both errors high and close (high bias). The deep tree has tiny training error but huge validation error (high variance). The regularized boosting model keeps both errors low with a small gap.

items: Check absolute training performance — poor training performance suggests high bias.
Compare training and validation — a large gap suggests high variance.
Select the model with the best cross-validated performance, not the best training score.
Confirm the final choice once on a separate test set not used for tuning.

content.caption: Figure 4. Typical score patterns: a very simple model scores low on both (0.70/0.68); a balanced model scores high on both (0.90/0.88); a very complex model scores near-perfect on training but drops on validation (0.99/0.72).

content.text: Diagnosing from scores

rows: Data quality, leakage, imbalance, or pipeline issue

content.text: A small training-validation gap does not automatically mean the model is good — both scores may be equally poor because of high bias.
content.title: Diagnostic caution

content.text: How to reduce high bias

rows: Gives access to missing predictive signals.
Add location, age, area for price.
Lets parameters fit the data more freely.
More weak learners cut residual systematic error.
Makes the pattern easier to learn.

content.text: How to reduce high variance

rows: Reduces dependence on a small/unusual sample.
Averages unstable models to lower variance.
Fewer chances to learn accidental patterns.

content.text: Regularization and the trade-off
Regularization intentionally restricts the model. It often increases bias slightly but can reduce variance substantially, giving lower validation error overall.
Algorithm tendencies

rows: Lower variance than a single deep tree
Number and diversity of base learners
Often reduces bias, may overfit if pushed
Learning rate, depth, estimators, early stopping

content.text: Role of cross-validation
Cross-validation estimates how a model performs across different training samples — directly helping identify variance and tune complexity.

items: Large variation in scores across folds indicates instability and possible high variance.
Consistently poor scores across folds indicate high bias or weak features.
Tune tree depth, k, polynomial degree, and regularization using validation or cross-validation.
The test set should remain untouched until the final model is selected.

content.caption: Figure 5. A practical diagnosis cycle: train → compare training and validation → diagnose bias or variance → apply a correction and re-evaluate, using cross-validation until performance is stable.

content.text: Connection with learning curves

rows: Train and validation errors converge high
Richer model, better features, or less regularization.
Train error low but validation much higher
Add data, regularize, simplify, or average.
Validation keeps improving with more data
Keep the model and confirm on the test set.

content.text: Common misunderstandings

rows: “A more complex model is always better.”
Complexity cuts bias but may raise variance and test error.
Training error can fall while validation error rises.
More data mainly helps variance, not strong bias.
A small bias increase can be worth a larger variance drop.
Here it means systematic prediction error — fairness bias is separate.
A single split can mislead; cross-validation is more stable.

content.text: Quick comparison
Practical checklist

items: Evaluate both training and validation metrics.
Use cross-validation instead of relying on one split.
Check both the score level and the training-validation gap.
Tune complexity-controlling hyperparameters.
Use pipelines to prevent data leakage.
Inspect learning curves when diagnosis is unclear.
Report mean cross-validation score and its variability.
Evaluate the final selected model once on the held-out test set.

content.text: Final takeaways

items: Bias is systematic error; variance is sensitivity to the training sample.
Underfitting is mainly high bias; overfitting is mainly high variance.
Increasing complexity normally lowers bias but raises variance.
The best model has the lowest reliable validation/test error, not the lowest training error.
Cross-validation, learning curves, regularization, data collection, and model simplification manage the trade-off.

content.text: High bias means the model is too rigid to learn the signal; high variance means the model is too flexible and learns noise.
content.title: One-sentence memory rule

content.text: Mini self-check

1. 98% training accuracy and 72% validation accuracy — likely problem? 2. Both training and validation accuracy around 65% — likely problem? 3. What usually happens to bias as complexity increases? 4. What usually happens to variance as complexity increases? 5. Why can regularization improve test performance? 6. Which metric should guide model selection: training or cross-validated score?
content.title: Test yourself

content.text: Answers

items: High variance / overfitting.
High bias / underfitting (assuming the task allows better performance).
Bias generally decreases.
Variance generally increases.
It reduces variance, even though it may increase bias slightly.
Cross-validated performance should guide selection.

keyPoints: Expected test error decomposes into Bias² + Variance + Irreducible noise; the first two trade off against each other.
High bias (too simple) gives poor, close training and validation scores; high variance (too complex) gives a great training score and a large validation gap.
As complexity rises, bias falls and variance rises, so expected test error is U-shaped — the minimum is the best trade-off.
Cut bias with more capacity/features/less regularization; cut variance with more data, regularization, simplification, pruning, and averaging.
Select by the lowest reliable cross-validated error — not the lowest training error — and confirm once on an untouched test set.
commonMistakes: Assuming a more complex model is always better, ignoring the variance it adds.
Selecting the model with the lowest training error instead of the best validation performance.
Expecting more data to fix a high-bias model (it mainly helps variance).
Reading a small train-validation gap as success when both scores are actually poor.

lessons.title: Baseline Models
lessons.summary: Why every candidate model needs a simple reference to beat, and how to build one fairly. Covers the definition and types of baseline (no-skill, simple learned, operational, domain), why they matter, task-specific baselines for classification (majority/stratified/prior), regression (mean/median/quantile), and time series (naive/seasonal-naive/drift), a fair validation workflow and pseudocode, three worked examples (student-risk, house-price, demand forecasting), interpreting absolute vs relative improvement, common mistakes, and a checklist.

content.text: The control condition of machine learning

An accuracy of 81% sounds good — until you learn a trivial rule already scores 80%. A baseline model is the reference that gives every other score its meaning: the minimum bar a real model must clear before you can claim it has learned anything useful.

content.caption: Figure 1. The performance ladder: a model should climb from a trivial baseline, past a simple learned baseline and a candidate model, to a production model — moving up only when the improvement is validated, relevant, stable, and worth the cost.

content.text: A baseline model is the minimum reasonable performance standard that a new model must beat under the same evaluation conditions.
content.title: One-sentence summary

content.text: These notes stay focused on baseline models as reference points for evaluating and validating ML models.
content.title: Scope

content.text: Learning goals

items: Define a baseline model and explain why it is required before accepting a complex model.
Select suitable baselines for classification, regression, and time-series forecasting.
Compare baseline and candidate models using appropriate validation methods and metrics.
Identify misleading baselines, data leakage, and unfair comparisons.

content.text: Definition and core idea

A simple reference model used to judge whether a more advanced model has learned useful patterns — it may predict using only the target distribution, a simple rule, a previous observation, or a low-complexity algorithm.
Formally, if M₀ is the baseline and M₁ the candidate, the candidate is useful only when its validation performance is meaningfully better than M₀ on the metric that matters.
A baseline is not the same as a bad model

items: No-skill baseline: uses little or no feature information (e.g. always predict the majority class).
Simple learned baseline: a transparent algorithm such as linear or logistic regression.
Operational baseline: the current business rule, manual process, or production system.
Domain baseline: a credible expert rule, such as “tomorrow will equal today” in forecasting.

content.caption: Figure 2. Rules of thumb: start with a trivial no-skill predictor (it exposes class imbalance), add a simple learner to check for basic signal, and compare fairly with identical folds, preprocessing, and metrics.

content.text: Why baseline models matter

rows: Whether features carry signal beyond a trivial rule.
81% accuracy isn't impressive if the majority baseline scores 80%.
When accuracy is inflated by a dominant class.
Predicting all patients “healthy” has high accuracy, zero disease recall.
A clear threshold for model acceptance.
A demand forecast should beat the previous-period forecast.
Prevents needless use of expensive models.
Prefer a linear model if a neural net gains only 0.2% RMSE.
A sub-baseline candidate hints at leakage or bugs.
Negative R² means worse than predicting the mean.
“Recall rose from 0% to 70%” is clearer than one score.

content.text: Main types of baselines

content.caption: Figure 3. The task type determines both the baseline and the most informative metrics — classification, regression, and time series each have their own defaults.

rows: Predict the most common training label.
Sample labels by training class proportions.
Always predict a chosen critical class.
Predict the training mean (MSE/RMSE, R² baseline).
Predict the training median (strong for MAE).
Use one or a few features to check basic signal.
Next value = value from the same prior season.
The current rule or deployed system.

content.text: Classification baselines
Majority-class baseline

The majority-class baseline predicts the most frequent training label for every observation. It is easy to compute and especially useful for revealing imbalance — but can reach deceptively high accuracy while failing completely on the minority class.
With 800 safe and 200 at-risk students, predicting “safe” for everyone gives 80% accuracy but 0% recall for at-risk students.
content.title: Imbalanced example

content.text: Other dummy strategies

rows: Class probabilities equal to training priors.
Useful for log loss / probability benchmarks.
Represents chance under the observed distribution.
Pure chance reference for balanced classes.
Tests behaviour for a critical class.

content.text: Strong simple classification baseline

After a dummy baseline, a simple logistic regression is a stronger learned baseline: it uses the features, trains fast, produces probabilities, and is interpretable. A complex classifier should normally beat both the dummy and the simple learned baseline.

content.caption: Figure 4. Why accuracy alone can mislead: the majority baseline (800/0/200/0) detects none of the 200 at-risk students, while the candidate (700/100/60/140) detects 140.

content.text: For imbalanced classification, compare recall, F1, balanced accuracy, and PR-AUC — not only overall accuracy.
content.title: Metric lesson

content.caption: Figure 5. On the imbalanced student-risk task the majority baseline scores 0% precision/recall/F1 despite 80% accuracy, while the candidate reaches recall 70% and balanced accuracy 78.8%.

content.text: Regression baselines
R² = 0 means performance equal to the mean baseline; R² < 0 means the model is worse than predicting the training mean for every case.
content.title: R² interpretation

content.caption: Figure 6. Illustrative house-price errors (lower is better): the mean/median baselines sit near MAE 49–52, while linear regression (35) and random forest (28) show real signal.

content.text: Time-series baselines
Time-series models must be compared with forecasting rules that respect temporal order. Random train-test splitting is usually inappropriate because it can let future information influence training.

rows: Extend the average change over time

content.caption: Figure 7. A forecasting model must beat credible naive and seasonal references — here the seasonal reference tracks actual demand more closely than the previous-month naive.

content.text: Evaluate with walk-forward validation or an expanding/rolling window. The baseline and candidate must be tested on exactly the same forecast periods.
content.title: Time-series validation

content.text: Fair baseline validation workflow

content.caption: Figure 8. The workflow: define the task → choose a simple baseline → validate fairly (same split, folds, metrics) → train the candidate → keep only meaningful, reliable improvement.

items: Define the target, prediction horizon, and decision the model will support.
Choose the primary metric before examining model results.
Create a trivial baseline that uses no feature signal.
Create a simple learned baseline when appropriate.
Use the same train/validation/test split or CV folds for every model.
Fit preprocessing only on training data, inside a pipeline.
Report mean score and variability across folds, not only one split.
Evaluate the final selected model once on an untouched test set.
Check whether the gain is practically useful and worth added cost, latency, and complexity.

content.text: Pseudocode pattern

content.code:
1. Split data (or create cross-validation folds)
2. Fit baseline on training data only
3. Predict the validation fold
4. Fit candidate model using the same fold
5. Predict the same validation fold
6. Compute identical metrics
7. Repeat for all folds
8. Compare mean score, variability, and practical cost

content.text: Worked examples
A. Student-risk classification
Predict whether a student is at risk of failing (positive = “at risk”). Of 1,000 test students, 200 are at risk and 800 safe.
The candidate improves accuracy by only 4 percentage points, but its real value is detecting 70% of at-risk students versus 0% for the baseline.
content.title: Conclusion

content.text: B. House-price regression
Predict house price (test errors in thousands of currency units):

Relative MAE improvement of the random forest over the mean baseline = (52 − 28) / 52 × 100 ≈ 46.2%. The mean and median baselines are near the no-skill reference; linear regression and random forest show that features carry real signal.
C. Monthly demand forecasting

A forecasting model reports MAE = 8.2. The last-value baseline has MAE = 9.0, but the seasonal-naive baseline has MAE = 7.6. The model beats the naive baseline yet fails to beat the stronger seasonal one — so it should not yet be accepted.
content.title: Beat the strongest credible baseline

content.text: Interpreting improvement

Absolute improvement = candidate − baseline (for higher-is-better metrics): e.g. F1 rising 0.61 → 0.66 is a 0.05 gain. Relative error reduction = (baseline error − candidate error) / baseline error × 100: e.g. RMSE 68 → 39 is about 42.6%.

rows: Is the average CV score better?
Is the gain consistent across folds/seeds?
Translate into cases detected, cost saved, delay reduced.
Is the gain worth time, latency, memory?
Prefer the simpler model when effectively tied.
Does it hold across subgroups and time?
Do subgroup, drift, and stress checks.

content.text: Do not select a complex model merely because its score is numerically higher — select it when the gain is reliable, decision-relevant, and worth the added complexity.
content.title: Selection principle

content.text: Common mistakes and best practices

rows: Using test-set info to build the baseline
Differences may come from easier/harder samples.
Use identical folds and test periods.
Hides total failure on a minority class.
Add recall, F1, balanced accuracy, PR-AUC.
Include both trivial and strong simple baselines.
Use fixed seeds and repeated validation.
Fit transformations inside a training pipeline.
A model may beat a dummy but not the current process.
Compare with the existing rule or system.
Added complexity may not be justified.

content.text: Baseline checklist

items: Baseline is defined before final model selection.
Baseline parameters are estimated from training data only.
Candidate and baseline use identical validation folds.
Metric matches the real decision cost.
Both trivial and strong simple baselines are considered.
Score variability is reported.
Operational cost and practical impact are discussed.
